div.head: INFANTILE MORTALITY. Bad Motherhood and Artificial Feeding.
div.p: INFANTILE MORTALITY. Bad Motherhood and Artificial Feeding.
Paper by Dr. Gaffikin.

" Some Causes of Infantile Mortality "was the sub- ject of a paper contributed by Miss Prudence E. Gaffikin, the acting medical officer of health for Warrington, at the Congress of the Royal Institute of Public health at Douglas on Tuesday. Mr. John Burns, she said, had attributed the high death-rate of infants to bad motherhood. Bad motherhood was rarely wilful ; it was generally due to ignorance. This ignorance existed not only with regard to ordinary care of infants, but as to the deleterious effects of soothing syrups and patent foods. Babies were regularly dosed with opium in one form or other in the belief that it was doing them good. With regard to another class of drugs—abortifaoients—the use of which was daily becoming more widespread, it was doubtful whether the mothers sinned in ignorance; but in the majority of cases they did not realise the full extent of the damage done to an infant's health where they were used and failed in effect. During the last six months the number of still and premature births in Warrington, due chiefly to abortifacients, was heart-breaking. The remedy for these dangers to infant life and health was to be found in the prohibition of the sale of all sooth- ing syrups, teething powders, opiate preparations, and abortifacients without a doct4r's prescription; the teaching of schoolgirls in the management of babies— lessons which would be worthless without an extension of the school age—and the training of midwives, so that they could advise mothers. Midwives needed particularly to be given better training, especially as regarded the feeding of infants. This ignorance was shown by the fact that fully one-half of the deaths of children under one year were to be attributed to troubles arising from food. The diarrhcea diseases alone accounted for fully one-third of the total infantile death-rate. To secure greater cleanliness in the food and surroundings of infants epidemic diarrhcea should be made a notifiable disease. Women's labour had been described by Mr. John Burns as an individual mistake, a social tragedy, and a communal blunder; but until some means was devised of preventing it with- out inflicting injustice the problem of nurse children was not to be escaped. It was quite fallacious to argue that a sensible woman would see that her child was given into safe keeping. She was not a free agent in this matter. Her choice was limited ; she must take what she could get. The State had already acknowledged its responsibility by passing the Infant Life Protection Act : but it had proved to be worse than useless, for while five-sixths of nurse and adopted children did not come under it at all, its provisions actually suggested to evil-doers methods of escape from its penalties. In Dresden a Very complete system of inspection of foster childrenhad been in force for many years, and some such system was needed in all our large manufacturing towns, vghere women were much employed outside their homes. Dr. Snell (Coventry) contributed a paper on the same subject, and gave a local sample of the pernicious work done by Me-, in the spreading of diarrhceal epidemics as a proof of the necessity for the removal of decompos- able animal and vegetable matter on which the flies could breed. Dr. Buchan (St. Helens) disagreed with the opinion that insanitation was a special cause of infantile mortality. Dr. Utting (Liverpool) endorsed Miss Gaffikin's con- demnation of potent sedatives administered to babies, and said the trouble was infinitely more prevalent than was imagined. He believed also that the filthy, beastly, and detestable thing known as the " dummy " was a frequent contributor to diarrhcea. (Hear, hear.)

£B,OOO DAMAGES TO ONE iAN. A TRAM SMASH WHICH HAS ENTAILED A TWO-SHILLING RATE. . _ . .

----- -- A verdict for £B,OOO damages was given at Bristol Assizes on Wednesday in favour of Mr. Richard Towns- end, corn and seed merchant, of Chalford, Gloucester, who brought an action against the Corporation of Swindon for damages for personal injuries snstained in the tramcar accident at Swindon during the Bath and West of England Show there last week.—The evidence showed tbat before the accident plaintiff was a robust man of exceptional business capabilities, and he was now described as a complete wreck.—The compensation paid by the Swindon Corporation in connection with the accident, in which four people were killed and many injured, has entailed a 2s. rate on the ratepayers of Swindon.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
FETTERS OF FAsmps.

The modern craze for over-dressing lies at the root of this evil—as it does with so many others, says London Opinion. The modern woman is fettered by fashion. How can she attempt to battle with the slightest puff of wind when wear- ing a picture hat laden with immense feathers that the slightest draught must necessarily dis- arrange—let alone attempt to walk even the length of Bond-street while holding up a chiffon gown that measures ten or twelve yards round the hem—and at the ' same time strive to control a floating scarf that threatens to strangle the unwary passer-by? The fact is, dress is made to be admired and not to be put to any utilitarian purpose nowadays. The woman of fashion clothes herself for effect rather than warmth or comfort, and is quite content to put up with a hundred inconveniences rather than to be out of the fashion.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The German Emperor, of whom it is said that there is practically nothing he cannot do, has a very accom- plished sister-in-law in Princess Fedora of Schlesung- Holstein, who has recently published her first novel entitled "Hahn Berta." She is the youngest sister of the German Empress, and has written other books, but "Hahn Bertha," a story of a poacher and his daughter.' is her first novel. Although she has had deep sorrows, Princess Fedora always looks upon the bright side of the picture of life, and is a great favourite of the Kaiser. Unlike many royalties, who are ready to change their religion if necessary,she refused to become a Roman Catholic, but had she done,so Princess Fedora might have been Queen of Italy. Since the death of her finance, Duke Frederick of Mecklenburg-Schwerin who was drowned at sea whilst in command of a torpedo boat, she has persisteatly refused all offers of marriage., The end of Runaway Marriages.—The present year is rich in jubilees and centenaries, and somebody who wishes to add one more to the number, has pointed out that it is fifty years since the irregular marriages at Gretna Green were declared invalid. These marriages, which took place in the presence of the village black- smith, consisted of a declaration of the parties that they took each other for man and wife, and they caused the question to be raised in the English courts, whether even in England their validity ought not to be tried by ; the law of Scotland, where they were celebrated. The ' decision was in the affirmative, but the Act passed fifty years ago provided that no irregular marriages should be valid in Scotland, unless one of the parties had lived in Scotland for the twenty-one days next preceding the marriage, or had his or her usual residence there at the time. The hearing a great deal about accident insurance, and the coat we have sketched was carried out in Nattier- new domestic liability. Little else, in fact, is talked blue Shantung, and trimmed with some Oriental about, but an accident at Harlesden suggests that bargain-hunting at the summer sales, involves a danger that it would also be well to insure against. No doubt every woman is at heart a bargain hunter, and so fierce was the struggle at Harlesden, that one lady who was "knocked down and trampled upon," was removed to the hospital, "having sustained a fractured arm and leg, and serious internal injuries." Such incidents are more common in America than with us, but many fearful crushes have characterised the opening of the mid-summer campaign at the chief London houses. The "recent inclement weather" as the sale catalogues mildly describe it, has tended to greatly increase the aggregate of bargains and bargain-hunters, but, unless we are fully equal to the occasion, and women generally hunt in couples—one should beware of the vast crowds who sally forth evidently determined" to have a good time" at the summer sales. Concerning Bathing Suits.—Wonderful silk and satin bathing suits figure largely at the sales but needless to say such toilettes are only for those women who bob about in shallow water. For the girl or woman who swims, or even bathes seriously, a suit high to the neck, with no sleeves, or over-skirt, and the knicker portion coming not lower than two or three inches below the knees, is undoubtedly the best, and among the most "tried and true " materials, are ordidary house flannel, which can be trimmed with coloured braid, and navy- blue serge, which can be simply ornamented with yak lace. For the shore coat, in which the bather runs from the sea to her tent, any white woolen material can be used, and a capital plan is to take a very large square of the fabric, round off the corners, and cut a hole, through which to pop the head, in the centre, in much the same way we were want to do, in days gone by when preparing a skirt for sun ray pleating. Bathing is decidedly fashionable, and the girl or woman who declines to take her dip or swim in the sea during the summer holidays, is voted somewhat a coddle. Not all of us however, find ourselves better for sea bathing, and such individuals would do well to leave it alone. With regard to children,the child who turns blue and shivers, ought not to be compelled to bathe these symptoms 'being Nature's danger signals that the little one is unfit for the shock of the water. div.head: ALCOHOL IN ALL BREADS.
div.p: ALCOHOL IN ALL BREADS.

As flour undergoes fermentation in the pro- cess of leavening, it has been supposed flint a little alcohol might be retained in the loaf in spite of the oven's heat. This proves to be tha case, one German chemist having found from 0•2 to 04 of absolute alcohol in freshly- baked English bread, while another ob- tained a much smaller amount-o'os to 008 per cent.—from German wheat-bread. Be- sides the alcohol was found a little dark- brown oil, which had the odour characteristic of new bread.

div.head: CAST-IRON MAGNETS.
div.p: CAST-IRON MAGNETS.

It is known that chilled cast iron serves very well for making permanent magnets, and such magnets are much cheaper than those made of steel. Albert Campbell has experimented with cast-iron magnets, and has found that they compare favourably with magnets made of special steel. He heats the iron to about I,ooodeg. Centigrade, and then plunges it in cold water. But while such magnets may ansiver as a substitute for steel ones for many purposes, it is not yet certain that they can be made sufficiently constant and uniform in quality to be employed in electrical measuring instruments.

div.head: DO INSECTS SLEEP?
div.p: DO INSECTS SLEEP?

Insects do not sleep as we understand it, they have no eyelids. Consequentry, they are unable to close their eyes. But scientific ob- servers maintain that • day insects remain quiet at night, and those that work at night are tranquil throughout the day. So that to all intents and purposes they sreep, in that they rest at regular intervals. Whether they " sleep " in the sense of losing conscious- ness when resting there does not seem to'be any possible way of determining. Indeed, no means have yet been devised by which We can even ascertain how much consciousness insects possess when they are, so to speak, awake.

div.head: WEATHERING COAL.
div.p: WEATHERING COAL.

It is probably' not generally known that coal exposed to the atmosphere undergoes chemical changes greatly affecting its quality. Moisttire is the most powerful a'gent In producing sbch change. It is a matter of common knowledge among men engaged in the making of illuminating gas that coal which has been stored for a long time ex- periences a loss of hydrocarbons, and the effects of the change are sh'ewn in a 'diminu- tion of the volume of the ,coal and in a loss of illuminating power in the gas produced from it. Such chemical changes occurring in great masses of coal may even produce suffi- cient accumulation of heat to cause spon- taneous combustion.
EFFECTS OF LIGHT ON THE BLOOD.

Dr. Oerum, of the Finsen Institute at Copenhagen, has carried out ,a number of experiments on the effect of light on the blood, of which we give a few results. Dark- ness has been found to reduce the total amount of blood by 3 to 33 per cent., while decreasing at the same time the amount of blood contained in the heart. Red light will exert a similar action to darkness, while blue light is apt to result in an excess of blood, and an increase in the amount con- tained by the heart. Light baths are apt to increase the amount of blood in the course of four hours. Darkness will reduce the amount of blood contained in the heart within three to four weeks, and intensified light will have the same effect in four hours. Darkness will increase, and intensified light will reduce the blood pressure. Animals born in .the dark or in red light have a greater weight, but only half the amount of blood of those born under normal conditions.

div.head: SPEED OF EARTHQUAKES.
div.p: SPEED OF EARTHQUAKES.

The course which an earthquake runs is usually very rapid. From the instant when the first shock was felt at Lisbon to the period when all was over and many thou- sands of people killed, not more than two minutes had elapsed. Usually from, ten to thirty seconds elapse between the first and last shocks of severe earthquake. But this lightning speed is not alwayi the earth- quake's mode of travelling. While Caracas, in Venezuela, was almost totally dest'royed and 12,000 people were killed in less than twenty seconds by the great shock there many years back, there are cases in which con- stantly recurring shocks have lasted -for weeks. No matter how brief the span, the most frightful havoc can be wrought, and the wave of destruction propagated from the most distant regions. The rumbling earth sound travels at the rate of about 10,000 ft. to 11,000 ft. per second, and the earth wave, oq an average, about,' 1,200 ft. in the same space of time.

div.head: WINE AS A FOOD.
div.p: WINE AS A FOOD.

Wine in moderate doses is a food, declares the Hospital, from which there is practically no waste; it requires no digestion, and is rapidly absorbed from the stomach. Its food value as represented by the alcohol it con- tains is theoretically the greatet of any nutritive substance we possess, with the single exception of fat; and if we take into consideration the energy required to digest fat, the former is probably more economical. One gram of alcohol is capable of providing 7,184 calories, one gram of fat 9,300, one gram of proteid 5,711. Numerous experiment* have been made as to the effect of given quantities of alcohol upon the amounts of other foods required to constitute a typical diet, and it has been clearly shewn that alcohol is capable of actually replacing fat in the diet and of reducing the amount of proteid required. Alcohol is a food, and it can be taken in doses in which it acts only as a food; but in practical dietetics the actual food value of a wine is of secondary importance.

THE WEIGHT OF MAN ON THE PLANETS. If the planet Mars is really inhabited, the people who live there must be an exceed- ingly- nimble race, says Science Siftings. The average weight of a man is about 1401 b., but the force of gravity on Mars is so much less than on the earth that the 1401 b. man would weigh only 531 b. if he were transported there. With such light weight, and still re- taining the same strength, an individual would be able to run with the speed of an express train, go skipping over 10ft, walls, and do various other extraordinary things. On the moon, a man would be even lighter. But on the sun, our 1401 b. man would have his troubles'. Instead of being an airy in- dividual, he would weigh about a ton and three-quarters. He would probably have the greatest difficulty in raising his hand, for that member would weigh about 3001 b. Ac- cording to scientific computation, a man who On the earth weighs 1401 b. would on the other celestial bodies weigh, in pounds, as follows: Moon 23, Mars 53, Venus 114, Mer- cury 119, Neptune 123, Uranus 127, Earth 140, Saturn 165, Jupiter 371, Sun 3,871.

div.head: PROPERTIES OF NICKEL ALLOYS.
div.p: PROPERTIES OF NICKEL ALLOYS.

A valuable contribution to our knowledge of the properties of certain alloys of nickel is made by Mr. Bruce V. Hill in an article in the Physical Review. He points out that there are two classes of alloys 'of the ferro- magnetic metals which are of particular in- terest, the steels and the alloys used in the construction of resistances. The importance of the magnetic characteristics of steel hat; only been realised in recent times. It was thought until only a few years ago that the hardening of steel by sudden cooling was the result of strains set up in the metal, due to the rapid fall in temperature, which caused the hardness, or that this property was ac- counted for by the presence of small par. ticles of very hard carbon or carbide. But none of these facts explain the phenomena of the tempering of steel. In connection with these properties the author discusses the facts as to certain of the nickel alloys, and he gives the effects of various metals upon the transformation point of nickel. He sliews that the substances used for electrical resistances are mostly nickel alloys, the greater part of them being non-magnetic. 'who magnetic metals, if heated to a certain critical temperature become non-magnetic and exhibit a much higher specific heat, and a higher electric resistance, together with a cou,ch smaller temperature co-efficient,

div.head: PHYLLIS VERE'S PICNIC,
div.p: PHYLLIS VERE'S PICNIC,
BY MRS. LEYS,
Author of "Mrs. Featherstone's Flirtation,' "Her Guilty Secret," "'Twat Friend and Foe," "The Queen's Necklace," &c. • •

"I wish to change my book. Did you get me 'A Summer Shower ' ? ' Thank you." The girl took her novel from the clerk at the railway book-stall, and was about to leave the station when the five o'clock express from London came rushing in, and she paused involuntarily to watch the passengers alight. From a first- class compartment just opposite to her a young man emerged—a young man dressed in light summer tweeds, fresh and spotless as if he had just quitted his dressing-room. The girl sprang forward to meet him. "Oh, Digby ! I quite forgot you might be back by this train. What about the match?"
Flushed, eager, unconscious of her surround- ings, she poured forth questions, until the frown on the young man's face made her stop short. "Why, what's the matter ? "
At that moment two men in boating flannels rushed up, lifting their caps to the girl and echoing her questions about the great cricket match at Lord's.
"I'll see my cousin home first and meet you by the Bank directly," the young man said; and the girl, in answer to his gesture, left the station with him.

"I wonder if youll,ever. learn how to behave •svith ordinary propriety,l'hyllis ? "he said, coldly. "What do you mean?" "You might have had more sense than to come to meet my train, And you do look so untidy and heated You ought not to be out of the house at all on such an afternoon. I don't know what those fellows can think of you, always rushing about the town with nobody to keep you in countenance. I shall speak to aunt about you again. You are the talk of the place. What?" "I did not speak. lam waiting until you have said all you wish to." The girl's voice was very quiet, but her hazel eyes shot glances of defiance at the lecturer, and she pressed her lips tightly together as if to keep back the words that were ready to pour forth.

On the other side of the narrow street a lady was approaching, leaning on the arm of a soldierly-looking, middle-aged man. Her com- panion made some remark to her in a low tone as they came nearer which caused her to look intently at Phyllis, while he raised his hat and bestowed on the girl a look full, to an observant eye, of admiration and delight. Thus, however, it did not strike the irate Digby. "There ! " he cried, after they had passed. "Did you see that? Colonel Armitage was pointing you out to that lady, and I could see that they were both laughing at your extraordinary appear- ance. It's too bad of you, Phyllis, to disregard appearances as you do. If you don't mind on your own account, you might at least remember that those connected with you don't care to have you making yourself conspicuous." Phyllis stopped short. "Have you b quite done ? " she asked, her voice trembling with anger.

"No, I haven't. Only last evening I overheard some fellows—never mind who—talking about the hail-fellow-well-met way you have with men. They called it awfully jolly, but you know as well as I do what men think of girls who make themselves too cheap. it wasn't intended for me to hear, so I could not say anything; and I'm sure I don't know what I could have said. It was all so true. You seem to take a perfect pleasure in disregarding the conventionalities. I wonder you don't give parties on your own account and ask men to them."

"Thanks for the suggestion. I will! I wanted to think of something novel for my birthday, and that will just do. I'll give a picnic. The mothers never know what to do with themselves at a picnic, poor things—they are so afraid of spiders and ants! So I'll leave them out and invite just some girls and some men. I'm awfully obliged for the idea. I should never have thought of it myself, but it will do capitally. You shall have the first invitation."
"Thanks. _I shall have a.previous engagement."

"What a disappointment—for you! Wood-bye. No, thank you. I don't think any of my men friends are about, so I can go to the end of the road without your needing to fear that the family name will be dragged in the dust. But, before we part, it may interest you to know that I didn' t come to the station to meet you!"

And Phyllis turned and wzilked briskly away. "Poor Phyllis! I didn't know she had so much of the family temper. Thank goodness I'm free from it I'm glad I said what I did. The sooner she learns that I'm not going to let my future wife disgrace herself the better for us both. What a child she is! I believe she was half serious for the moment about her picnic ! " And with a patronising smile he began to walk towards the river.
On his way he encountered Colonel Armitage, alone this time.

The two men stopped to speak. "What have you done with your cousin?" said the elder man. "Sent her home to brush her hair. It's an awful pity that my aunt lets her run wild like that. I could see you were rather shocked at the sight of her just now:"

"Slicked? I Icrouldn't have Miss Vere different for the world. She is so charming in her simplicity and so unconscious of her beauty." "So far as to be utterly regardless of the effects of the summer sii on her complexion," laughed Digby. "Ah ! she need have none of those fears."

"Polite old humbug ! " said Digby to himself, as they separated. And he imagined the surprise which everybody would feel some day at the change in Phyllis after she had come for ever under his training hand.
"I hate him! I hate him! I hate him ! "
Phyllis burst into the pleasant room where her friend and visitor, Evelyn Lawrence, was sitting engaged In some dainty lace work, and stamped her little foot.

Evelyn looked up. She was a pretty girl, fair- haired and pink and white, always beautifully dressed, always self-possessed. Nothing in the world, no event, no person, could over have ruffled her composure, and nothing would have induced her to do as Phyllis had just done—rush out in the heat of a July afternoon with only a narrow-brimmed sailor hat on her head and no sunshade. She looked pro- vokingly cool in her blue linen gown with a cluster of pink roses at her breast, and Phyllis, with her red cheeks, ruffled hair, and flashing brown eyes, looked like a little Fury beside her. "What is the matter, Phil? How hot you are! And who has vexed you so? Whom do you hate ? "
"Why, Digby, of course. He is the very nastiest, horridest man in the world, and I wish to goodness I wasn't related to him!" "What has he done ?"

"What has he done? He has shewn himself to be the most suspicious, and at the same time the most conceited, man 1 ever saw. Fancy this, Evelyn! You know I said at lunch that I should finish my novel this afternoon and go and change it before tea? Well, I went, and as I was coming away the tea-time train came in and out jumped Digby. Would you believe it? He at once assumed that I had gone down to meet him! Those two Cambridge men who are staying with him met him—Eden, and that „conceited creature' the wrangler. So Digby walked me away as fast as he could, and read me a lecture all the way on the awful impropriety of my conduct both on this occasion and in general. Why, if he had been my--" Phyllis stopped short, blushing furiously. "Your fiance, as everybody imagines him to be," put in Evelyn. "Well, he isn't, and he never will be." "My dear Phil! You forget your uncle's will." "No I don't. I know exactly what he said, and it does not bind me to marry Digby." "'But if you don't you will lose your share of the fortune!"

"And what is that compared with being married to a man who provokes all your worst feelings and is always trying to put a curb on you? No! My uncle left his money between Dtgby and me on condition that we married each other, but if one was willing to comply and the other refused, the obedient one was to have all the money. I'm not going to spoil my life for so manLthousands. of ,pounds. _Di.gby, of course,

wouldn't be so imprudent! He has his title and the estate, and he needs all the money he can get. I suppose if I had been a perfect Gorgon he would have still been ready to obey Digby has never asked me to marry him. I suppose he's waiting until I have learnt to say Pa, prunes and prism,' but he may wait for ever, and I'll never be the sort of wax figure he wants for a wife."

"But what will your mother say ? " "She will thank me for saving her from having a prig for a son-in-law. Alreacbr he scolds her about me till he nearly reduces Ser to tears. And now I shall go and see her about my picnic." "What picnic ? " "Oh! the one I am going to have on my birth- day. Digby put it into my head. Will you come ? "
"Of course. I love a picnic." "There will be no chaperons. lam going to ask only my girl friends and all the bachelors I know in the town."

"Phyllis ! " "Quite true. Digby suggested it." "But he must have been joking ! " "Did you ever know Sir Digby Vere to make a -lest, Evelyn ? What an imputation ! " She ran away to put her arms round her invalid mother's neck and easily win from the fond, silly woman, who had never attempted to play the part of guardian to her fatherless girl, an easy consent to indulge her latest whim. Evelyn sat thinking after Phyllis had left her, with her elbows resting on the table and the tips of her slender white fingers pressed together in the becoming attitude she had seen Sir Digby admiring only the evening before. Yes, this perversity of pretty Phyllis suited her friend to perfection. She would dearly love to be Lady Vere, and the young baronet admired her immensei' r • but he was bound to propose to his cousin. If she rejected him he was free to choose his own wife, and Evelyn had little doubt on whom his choice would fall.

div.head: LATEST FASHIONS.
div.p: THE LATEST FASHIONS.

The summer season is now at its height, and fashion is evolving strange styles, says the Ladies' Tailor, from the multitude of designs prepared for her selection. The broad-shoul- dered effect is everywhere introduced, and the kimono sleeve worn , over another is frequently adopted.

div.p: All the rest of the afternoon Phyllis was busy writing her invitations. In Castleton, as in all provincial towns, the proportion of girls to young men was great, but at this time the town happened to be pretty full. It was a gay little place, having a sea-front as well as a river, and it was a favourite resort of cricketing men. The fact of there beinc, a camp about three miles away added to its attractions, and Phyllis had quite a long list of names from which to make a selection of guests. Her notes were addressed to some eight young men living in the town, and to five staying at Sir Digby Vere's house, the High Beeches; and she wrote to about twenty of her girl friends. Replies came very soon. Most of the girls accepted with a pleasure that was not merely formal; but two or three who had brothers declined, and of the young men all, with one exception, sent excuses. Phyllis opened her cousin's note first, and found that almost every one of the answers was modelled on his—all pleading previous engagements. The solitary acceptance came from the curate. "Well," said Phyllis to hereslf, "I must make him go as far as I can. He's big enough, and very jolly. I'll get him to sing Father O'Flynn , but it looks very much as if the affair would degenerate into a sort of Penny Reading out of doors instead of in the school-room. Shall I try the Colonel ? " .

I Her decision cost her some minutes of reflec- tion, but at last she made up her mind to invite Colonel Armitage. Of course it was risking another snub, but the Colonel was always so kind and—and—nice to her. Her heart beat a little faster as she thought of him. At any rate, she did not think he would hurt her feelings if he • could help doing so. So she wrote him a grace- ful little note, and then proceeded to make a list of the men who had so cavalierly refused her invitation.

"Wait till the winter comes, my friends," she said to herself; "not one of you shall put your name on my programmes ! " And as Phyllis was not only the belle of the Castleton dance, but the best dancer, this threat meant a good deal. Almost as soon as the invitation could have reached him the Colonel's reply was brought back by his orderly. He accepted the invitation with expressions of gratification at being held worthy to be present on such a happy occasion, and asked whether Phyllis would further extend her kindness by allowing him to bring a friend with him. She wrote a hurried reply while the orderly waited, asking him to bring as many of his friends as would care to come; and as this, she knew, would almost certainly mean one or two of the young officers from Herncliffe Camp coming, her spirits rose high. Her girl friends would not have such a dull time after all, and she might be able to exact a little less from the curate. She ran off to tell the good news to Evelyn, but before She could speak her friend said:

"Oh! Phil, I wanted to see you. I've just had a note from my old governess asking me to spend a day or two in town with her at the beginning of next week. I don'tolike to hurt her feelings, poor old thing, so I'm afraid I'll have to miss the picnic." "Must you ? "
"I realty think I must." "Well, it would have been dull for you, of course." "Not at all."
But Phyllis fancied she read relief in Evelyn's manner, and, a little piqued, made no further reference to the picnic.

Phyllis felt a little anxious when her party assembled at the boating place.. The girls flocked together like frightened doves. The curate, in a blue and yellow blazer, ran hither and thither, eager to render yeoman service, and suggesting an arrangement of tying the four boats together in a queue so that he, sculling or poling the first one, might tow them all up the stream. But Phyllis assured him such a sacrifloe was quite unnecessary. "Some of the men here will row us to the island," she said. "The provisions have been sent up already, and the rest of our party are coming from higher up, so they will meet us at the island."

"I thought it was all nonsense when Edith Henderson told me there were to be no chaperons," whispered one girl to another. "She wasn't invited, so I fancied it was only a bit of spitefulness on her part." "I don't see that it matters," returned her friend, "seeing that there are no men. But it will be awfully slow." Phyllis read their looks, but said nothing. Her hope lay in Colonel Armitage. When they came in sight of the island a little nutter was seen to stir the occupants of the boats, for there, waiting to receive them, were several men and a grey-haired lady, _ _

• "Who are they ?-" someone asked. "Colonel Armitage and some of the officers from Herneliffe," said Phyllis, calmly, but she felt inclined to laugh aloud for joy. After all, her party was going to be a success. "Bad manners for us to be here first," said the Colonel, handing Phyllis out, "but I thought we might rig you up a tent or two, and help to pull up your boats." "You are too kind," said Phyllis, lifting to him eyes that had a suspicion of a tear in them, and the look which the Colonel returned could

; hardly be called paternal. "You gave me leave to bring a friend," said Colonel Armitage, turning to the lady who stood on the bank; "this is my sister, Lady Dinneford." I "My husband and your father were brother officers in India, my dear," said Lady Dinneford, embracing Phyllis. "I am very glad to know you.,,
After this there was a great deal of introduc- ing, and Phyllis had the satisfaction of seeing her dovelike companions all at once transformed into humming birds.
1 Phyllis's luncheon was a great success. It had been supplied by the best confectioner and ' caterer in Castleton, and was both recherché and t profuse. _ _

- Ices were going round when the sound of oars drew the attention of the revellers to the water, and three boats full of men came swinging round the island. The two parties recognised each other—apparently Sir Dibgy Vere and his pay- tien;iir friends were also picnicking, for their boats contained divers hampers. I To Phyllis's great aelight the person on whom Sir Digby's inquiring glance fell was the elderly lady sitting at her side. He could not conceal the astonishment he felt at seeing that his cousin was not only provided with male guests but that she was properly supported by a chaperon, and Phyllis liked to think that she saw envy written on the faces of the ungallant youths who, to please Sir Digby Vere, had condemned themselves .to a bachelor 'party.

She turned to Lady Dinneford and whlsperea "I can't thank you enough for coming. I know it can be no pleasure to you. But how could you know I wanted you?" "It was my brother, dear. We heard all about it at the camp—how your cousin, as it were, defted you, and of the idea you took into your mischievous head! My brother was determined that your party shouldn't be spoilt, so he insisted on forcing my company on you." "He is very good," murmured Phyllis. "He is years and years younger than me—l have always been a sort of mother to him, and I was very pleased to play the same part to you. I hope you'll let me do so again, often! And, I assure you, I'm enjoying myself immensely, as everyone else is. My brother looks quite boyish to-day. Now, Leslie, you must shew Miss Vere that view you wanted to sketch. lam going to pretend to read my magazine, but I feel rkther drowsy."

Next day Phyllis was lying in her hammock in the garden when she heard steps approaching, and, looking up, saw to her annoyance that it was her cousin who was coming towards her. She rose hastily with a little frown, and asked him how he came there. _

"I told Jenkins I was not at home to-day to anyone. lam tired." "I hope Jenkins would not have thought that this order applied to me, Phyllis? But I didn't give him a chance. I came round through the rose garden." Phyllis made no reply. Her cousin took her by the hand and led her to a seat under an overshadowing beech. "Can you guess what has brought me here to-day, dear ? " he said. She shook her head.

"Yesterday was your birthday,.but I wasn't able to see you then. We tdasted you at our feast, though! Well, I have come to give you my good wishes, and to ask you to accept this gift from me." He produced a ring ease, and, opening it, shewed her a very beautiful ring of diamonds and sapphires. "Do you like it ?" he said, softly. "It is very handsome." "Give me your hand, Phyllis, I wish to put it on—the left one, please." The girl clasped her hands together and shook her head.

"No, thank you, Digby. I do not wish to accept such a gift from you." "Don't you understand, Phyllis? I could not say it before—you were not old enough. But yesterday you were eighteen, and I am sure you will be as womanly and reserved now as a girl of your age ought to be. So I have come to ask you to marry me. Ido not think there is any need for so much formality, though, seeing that it has long been understood that we are to marry some day. "You are quite mistaken, Digby. I know that uncle wished us to be married, but only if we were both willing. Ido not want to marry you, so--what is the correct thing to say ?—I must decline your offer with thanks." She rose to put an end to the interview, but Digby, pale with wounded pride and surprise, did not move for a moment. Then he too rose, and took her hand.
"Phyllis, you don't mean this ? I never doubted that you would be willing to comply with our uncle's wishes. Do you know what your refusal will involve ? "

- "I know it means that I shall be almost penniless after mamma's death, as the bulk of her fortune goes to my step-brother. But what is that compared to marrying someone whom you—whom you don't care for ? " "I took it for granted---'1 "Ah! that is, a mistake. Uncle took it for granted too, it seems; but liking and loving cannot be taken for granted. It is very good of you, Digby, to mind at all. I know you are thinking that I shall suffer on account of my decision, but I am not at all afraid. And we shall be all the better friends for not being bound by anybody else's wishes in such a matter." "You are mistaken, Phyllis. I wish you could understand what a blow this is to me. And I can hardly take you seriously even now. I must see aunt."

"It is of no use, Digby. She agrees with me entirely. You and I could never have been happy together. I should have been shocking you constantly, and you—would have worried me!" "Well, Phyllis, I see it is of no use for me to say anything more at present. Only if you won't change your mind after a bit, you must let me make you an allowance."

"Nci, thank you; I never could accept that. Good-bye "—as her cousin held out his hand—"be happy! You have done your duty manfully." And she gave him the brightest smile she had had for him for many a day. Hardly an hour had passed when another visitor came, and at Phyllis's request was brought to her in the garden. "Oh, Colonel Armita,,e, I am so glad to see you! Ido want to than you for all your kind- ness yesterday." The Colonel took the two hands that she held out to him and kept them prisoners. "Who do you think is the one to be thankful P" he said. "I do not know when I have spent such a happy afternoon as I had yesterday, but the best part of my happiness lay in the hope of more to come. You were very good to me, little one. I know it is very presumptuous of me to dare to think that you might over come to care for me as I have long cared for you, but I can't wait any longer for a word of hope. My dear, you can't guess how much I love you! Do you think you could try to love me just a little to start with? I would be content to wait for more."
He bent his handsome head to catch the words that trembled on Phyllis's lips. "It doesn't need any trying. I didn't know uutil_now—but—l love you too!"
"My darling! You don't mind my being so much older ? "

"I like you all the better for that. You shall teach me to be wise. I'll try for your sake to gi ye up shocking everybody. "Don't try to be anything but what you are, dear—the most simple-minded, charming little NI itch in the world," and he clasped her to his breast.

Of course, all Castleton said that Phyllis's engagement to Colonel Armitage was a foregone conclusion after the picnic, and as he was a rich !Ilan nobody saw anything extraordinary in her - refusing her cousin. Sir Digby was able soon to Flew that he was not suffering from a broken heart by becoming engaged to Miss Lawrence, and so the conclusion of that episode in the history of a self-willed maid was satisfactory to ell concerned.
[TIIE END.]

WORKS EXCURSIONS FROM

Saturday was Warrington's annual trip day and in Connection with the various works numerous excursions to seaside resorts were organised. The result was that the town was almost deserted. On the whole the We!tther was favourable and the trippers spent a very enjoyable time.

div.head: Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, Ltd.
div.p: Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, Ltd.

Blackpool was again selected by the employees of the above firm for the annual trip on Saturday. The trippers numbered some 1,800, and were conveyed in trains supplied hy the Cheshire Lines Committee. This Was the-40th annual excursion, and was as enjoyable as anY which have preceded it. The weather was fine. All the usual places of intereSt were visited, and a very enjoyable day was spent. Mr. William Warburton Proved himself an efficient hon. secretary. Some 200 ef the visitors took advantge of the extension ticket and prolonged their stay in Blackpool over the week end,

CANON STEVENSON AND THE PROPOSED CONSCIENCE CLAUSE.

The PRINCIPAL said they had during the past week had the publication of the list of the preliminary certificate examination which qualified student i to enter the College, and it had been arranged for the first time on a different plan. it had appeared in alphabetical order without any classification, and consequently the College authorities had to deal with a list of many thousands of young people, most of Whom were anxious to enter some particular college, and they had no guide as to the merits of the candidates excepting the rather curious one of alphabetical order—(laughter)—and the fact that certain people had obtained distinction in certain sub- jects. The authorities' however, were not guided to a very great extent by the distinction marks—although they attached some importance to them—but% by the reports they received from the centres of the regular daily work of the students. Referring to a subject more intimately affecting the life of the college, Canon Stevenson said the building adjoining the school, formerly tenanted by the Clzrgy Daughters School, had been purchased and would be used to house a certain number of students. Hitherto students had been accommodated in two I hostels, one of which (Orford Hall) was at a considerable distance from the College. He thought it would be wiser that the Orford students should be accommodated under the same roof as the others. They hoped,although it would be premature to say anything definite that day, that there might be an educational future for Orford Hall, not directly in connection with the students of the College but in another manner.ln future the College would be brought into much closer connection with the Liverpool University. The three training colleges in the district—Chester, Warrington, and Edge Hill—were to be allowed to substitute for the examination of the Board of Education an examination to be conducted by the University of Liverpool. The sylla- buses would be drawn up by an examining board on which both the colleges and the University were repre- sented, and the examination would be equivalent in every respect to the Government certificate examination. This arrangement, which would come into operation after next September, was an experiment which was entirely new in this country, and one which he hoped would justify itself. Referring to Mr. M'Kenna's announcement that a con- science clause will be introduced into denominational colleges next year, Canon Morley Stevenson said there were ways in which a conscience clause could be intro- duced which might be perfectly justifiable, but there were ways in which it might so act as gravely to inter- fere with the unity of the college and its family life. He did not wish to approach the subject from any narrow point of view. He rejoiced to say they had Nonconformists among their day students in the college at the present time, and the system worked perfectly well. The college received a large sum from public money, and therefore they must be prepared to go a long way in that direction. "If some scheme can be elucidated," Canon Morley Stevenson continued, "by which those who are not members of the Church of England may receiiTe the benefits of a college such as this without interfering with the unity of the college itself I should welcome it. I do deprecate very strongly anything wl ich would introduce a divided camp within the walls of the college, which would compel us to send students of one denomination to worship in one direc- tion, and those of another denomination in another. Any such thing as that would break up the unity and destroy the corporate life of the institution, and would inflict upon colleges which have been built by friends of the denomination to which they belong and largely aided out of the funds of those friends from time to time in the faith that they were to be for the members of that denomination, a great injustice." BISHOP WELLDON & UNDENOMINATIONALISSI

Bishop WELLDON offered his congratulations to Canon Stevenson upon the remarkable success which had attended his administration of the college. (Applause.) He would like to impress upon the ladies who had chosen the noble vocation of teaching, the great interest and importance attaching to their work. Teachers and school managers wore apt to be impatient of the interference of the State—and he knew that interference was very often irritating—but after all it was a sign of the increasing value whic the State attached to the labours of teachers. The future of England depended in large raeasure upon the efficiency of the teachers, and he was surprised to see how little attention bad been paid to the training of teachers in secondary schools. Looking at educa- tional problems purely from the educational point of view, he desired that the teaching profession should be not only open but attractive to the best minds of all classes of the community. Every ster which tended to diminish the authority and dignity. of the teacher was a, loss to education. "It has," he added," been pro- posed on high authority to debar teachers in certain schools from giving religious instruction. In my opinion that is a fatal mistake. The privilege of teaching religion is often the strongest motive with the best persons to become teachers, and if you tell teachers they shall be shut out from giving instruction on the subjects they hold most dear you will drive away from the profession some of those who are capable of making the best teachers in the world. I would myself have never became a schoolmaster if I had not been allowed to teach ray boys at Harrow I religion. I will go a step further,although I come now to more debatable ground. lam a. person of broad educational sympathies and Ido not desire to take up an attidude of hostility to any branch of my fellow- Christians. I believe there is such a thing as common Christianity. One who has lived among the heathen as I have lived, cannot doubt that as there are certain persons who are called Christians in opposition to others wha are not Christians, so there is and must be a common element, great or small,which makes Christians Christians and distinguishes them from all other people. But human nature being what it is,l think you will not get the best results from the teachers if you don't allow them tl teach the full religion which they believe to be true. Whatever may be the difficulty of the problem that lies before the State,' cannot help holding that it ought not to be made impossible for any teacher to give denominational teaching, if he or she wishes to give it

which offer was refused. On the 9th of July, 1903 three directors of the Company met the Street Improvement Committee and offered to accept 1.2,500 for the whole of their premises or £5,000 for the strip required for the widening of the road. A sug- gestion was then made that the road should be widened on the other side which, apart from certain objectionable features, would not have relieved the Corporation from purchasing a slice of the Mersey Bedstead Company's premises and the slice which the Company had all along contended was the most valuable to them, The cost of widening on the opposite side of the road would have been as great, if not greater, than the cost of widening through the company's premises. There would have been three licensed houses to

• purchase. The most objectionable feature would have been the two kinks or dog legs which would have spoiled the improvement and obstructed the view. The buildings standing to the front of the Bedstead Company's land greatly obstruct the view, and the drivers of cars at Warrington Bridge connot see the and of-the buildings. The road is exceedingly narrow and very dangerous, especially to children. St. James's schools are only just off the main road.—Resuming his speech, Alderman Bennett said that for years it had been one of their great ideas to get hold of the property and proceed with the widening of Knutsford-road. When the Corporation were only asked for £l,OOO more than they were asked for a narrow strip- before, it seemed that they were getting the property dirt cheap. They were told that if they did not acquire it, they would not have the chanCe very long, as others were prepared to buy it at a high price. The Council would be more foolish than he liked to imagine possible to neglect the opportunity. Councillor Wilkinson got more difficult to understand at each Council meeting. (Laughter.) How he could take the line he did, know- ing the history of the transaction, he (Alderman Bennett) failed to understand. Councillor Wilkinson had acted in a most inconsistent and illogical manner, and he (Alderman Bennett) was surprised at him. Councillor WrLKlxsox said Alderman Bennett charged him with inconsistency. His changes, however k were caused by circumstances over which he had no control. I it was true the Corporation in days gone by wished to purchase a strip of the works and were willing to give £3,000. Alderman Bennett did not tell them that the £3,000 included the pulling down of part of the premises and the rebuilding, which made a big difference. The Council would be well advised to allow the matter to simmer a little longer. If anyone did start a works there and sent in plans of alterations the Council would be able to tell him they had prescribed a building line. Would they have to pay £3,000 then? No. Councillor WILDING said Alderman Bennett had not given them any conditions whatever. According to the advertisement, the purchaser had to buy the business at valuation.
Alderman BENNETT : No, we are buying the premises The INEAvoR : We are simply buying the premises and the land.
COUnCiiioi TOOLE thought the clauses governing the purchase should be read.

The MAYOR: The only thing there is in the matter is that there are other are other people who want to buy the property. Alderman TECNION said the Street Improvement Com- mittee had tried for years to purchase the property,and he did not hesitate to say that if they had given the sum they proposed to give for the strip of land, looking at the price they were now offering for the whole of the land, it would have been excessively dear. There were members of the Street Improvement Committee present who were parties to offering £3,000 for the strip of land alone. They wanted the property and must have it at some time or other, because they would not be so foolish and stupid as to widen the road to that point and leave the narrow and dangerous part as it was. Thelcon- ditions, as far as he understood them, were that they bought the land and buildings and there was no good- will or anything else to be purchased. Alderman FORSHAW : It is already sold. Alderman TeisroN said the business, as far as he understood it, had been sold. The question was whether the property was worth the amount to the Corporation for improvement purpmes. It did not matter to him whether the Town Clerk purchased it or not. The Town Clerk had made some very good bargains; he might also have made some bad ones.He believed the purchase was straightforward and above board. People would be prepared to buy the property, knowing that the Corporation would have to purchase it later, and they could create a business and a value for which the Cor- poration would have to pay. If the case went to arbitration it would no doubt cost the Corporation considerably more. He was given to understand that the amount offered was fair and reasonable and that the Corporation where making a bargain. Councillor TOOLE said that to use a common expres- sion, it seemed to be a rotten way of doing business to publicly discuss the price they were going to offer for the property. It was stated that there were three or four other parties seeking to purchase it. They all knew that people who had property to sell did not, offer it from philanthropic motives towards the Cor- poration. Personally he would not like to be a party to deprive the town of the improvement. The MAYOR said the matter was no secret. It was thoroughly discussed by the General Purposes Com- mittee.

ber of the Council should have an opportunity of dis- cussing in detail every phase of the purchase. The question of widening Black Bear Bridge had been dis- cussed for seven or eight years. The idea was to acquire property on each side the canal and to widen the bridge. There were, of course, many difficulties in the way, and up to the present time the Street Improvement Com- mittee had failed to accomplish the widening of the bridge in question. He submitted that the question of the purchase of these properties might be withdrawn and submitted to the General Purposes Committee with the fullest possible information. Alderman BENNETT said he had no objection. He had no desire to do anything surreptitiously, but the Street Improvement Committee was the committee which was supposed to consider questions of this kind, and it ought to have sufficient common-sense to be able to buy property with discretion. It was reducing their functions to a nullity. The minute about the purchase of the properties was withdrawn. The other minutes were agreed to. MERSEY BEDSTEAD WORKS. THE CORPORATION'S OFFER. div.head: RIVALS IN DEATH.
div.p: RIVALS IN DEATH.

A dispute betvveen two women for the possession of a man's body was brought under the notice of the West London magistrate on Wednesday. The wife of the deceased, who was living with another woman at the time of his death, asked that the body should be delivered up to her. The other woman refused to give the body to her. The magistrate, who observed that it was one of the most singular cases he had ever heard of, sent an officer to try to persuade the woman to give up the body.

THE Income Tax was the THE INCOME subject of discussion in the TAX. House of Commons on

Wednesday. Mr. ASQUITH again found it necessary to repudiate the state 1 ment that he has spok3o of a shilling in.the pound 1 lUCOITIO Tax as a permanency. Their is nobody, it is probable,who believes that he ever said anything to that effect ; but it is sometimes politically useful to pretend, just as children pretend when they are playing games with each other. And so, in spite of repeated contradictions, the Conservative party has gone on pretending, for purely party purposes, that the CHANCELLOR of the ExCHEQUER once said something or other that he never did say, and that is not the least in harmony with his views of national finance. That steward of the nation's finances who should declare that the income tax can never again fall below a shilling in the pound—even excepting earned incomes up to a certain amount, as Mr. Asquith does—would speedily be deposed, to whichever party he might belong, in favour of some financier with a more optimistic outlook. Mr. VICTOR CAVENDISH would certainly not be pounced upon as a possible successor to a Chancellor of the Exchequer who entertained such doleful views. -The heir to the DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE said on Wednesday that he accepted Mr.`AsQuirft's statement that he had no intention of making a shilling Income Tax an into gral part of our fiscal system, but he failed to see how it could be avoided. It certainly could by no means be avoided if the party to which Mr. CAVENDISH belongs were again in power. Were the nation to be speedily overtaken by such a calamity as the restoration of Conservative rule, it is pro- able that we should soon be looking back to a shilling Income Tax as a wholly desirable burden. Little more than thirty years have passed since Mr. GLADSTONE found it possible, if the country had been willing, to abolish the Income Tax altogether. Less than ten years later, the Government of the day was overthrown because it had brought in what was called the hundred million Budget. In 1874 it was necessary- to raise only 74 millions by means of taxation, and the abolitisn of the Income Tax was possible. We 1 now spend more than double that amount, and we have the Income Tax at a shilling in the pound. IWhat is the explanation? it is not hing more nor less than three long spells of Government by the Conservatives.

The country, it is to be feared, pays nothing like the requisite amount of attention to its own financial affairs. If it did so there would be less groaning under burdens and more determination to rednce them. When the Income Tax was introduced under Sir ROBERT PEEL, it was a temporary expedient. It was made a permanent method of raising taxation by the Crimean War , Chancellors of the Exc!iequer have found it to be 'by much the easiest niethod of raising revenue Where a penny in the pound formerly produced a million of pounds sterling, it now reaches two millions and a half or more. Even Mr. GLA.DSTONE, if he were now living, and if he wore in charge of the Exchequer, would not dream of abolishing. the Income Tax. But if he had remained per- manently in charge of the national finances, no such circumstances as those which now exist corrld

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 6, 1907

have arisen. If we were paying an Income Tax at all, we should be paying only a small one, and a hundred million Budget would still have continued to be a subject for alarmed surprise. But Mr. GLADSTONE was the great economist of the national finances. He made an enormous reduc- tion of the National Dent. That was one of the great objects of his Statesmanship. But under Conservative Government the debt has been increased to a point a little above what it stood at thirty years ago, and that is why the CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER finds it impossible for the present to place the Inco me Tax at less than a shilling in the pound.
A large number of the THE SMOKE members of the Warrington PROBLEM. Town Council still refuse

to seriously consider the smoke nuis once, notwithstanding the persistent appeals of Alderman Bennett. To their some- what unenlightened minds smoke, and plenty of it, from the factory and forge chimneys, spells good trade and prosperity. We do not deny that there is some ground for this conclusion, but it is surely not contended that the trade is dependent on the smoke? A number of enterprising firms—Messrs. Crosfield for one— have practically done away with smoky chimneys, and saved a large sum on coal consumption at the same time. Surely, if it pays, and benefits the community at the same time, other manufacturers should be inclined to follow the example set them. The " smoke " discussion at the Council meeting on Tuesday arose on the Medical Officer's report, and took the usual line. There was one unusual feature, how- ever, and that was a pronouncement from the only medical member, Dr. Joseph, who created surprise by saying that " he was extremeiy doubt- ful as to whether smoke was not absolutely good for the health of the town." Doubtless it does con- tain disinfectant qualities,but we think the worthy doctor ranged himself under the wrong banner. One illustzation alone is sufficient, in our opinion, to smash all arguments on behalf of smoke. A smoky atmosphere has not only a lot to do with the density and foulness of city fogs, but it obstructs the sunshine—and sunshine is life!

The fact that this import- THE NEW ART ant appointment,in addition MASTER. to the one at Beamont School, has been given by the School Management Committee to an outsider is responsible fora renewed feeling of dissatisfaction in local teaching circles. The appointment of Mr. C. Mawson Shipley) is not absolutely definite, inasmuch as it requires the confirmation of the full Education Committee at its next meeting on the 15th inst. From what we can learn there are good grounds for re-considering the present decision. An injustice appears to have been done to Mr. G. S. Pendlebury, the popular assistant art master, who is greatly sympathised with under existing circumstanc9s. The facts seem to be that Mr. Pendlebury applied in the first instance for the post to be vacated this month by Mr.Aylward,and was amazed to receive an official intimation that owing to the terms of certain regulations by the Board of Education the Committee was obliged to reject his application. Mr. Pendlebury at once communicated with the Board of Education, and received a reply from them that his qualifications were sufficient for the pr4st of principal teacher of a School of Art. Naturally, therefore, Mr. Pandlebury feels that he has not had a fair chance, and is petitioning for a reconsideration of the matter. Justice alone demands that theie facts should have proper weight with the Educa- tion Committee in deciding finally upon the appointment of aft master.

Warrington has made OUR SECOND NEW another advance in its SCHOOL. efforts to keep pace with the growing demands for educational accommodation, and yesterday witnessed the laying of the memorial stone of our second Council school which is to cater for the Latchford district. It was around the cost of thia school that so much discussion waged and after a determined fight the advocates of economy won the day. The result is that the bill which will be presented to the long- suffering ratepayer will be for 28,000—n0 doubt quite large enough for his liking but a sub- stantial reduction on the original figure. The Com- mittee has wisely determined that there shall be no useless ornamentation, but from the educa tional and health point of view—certainly the most important—there will be nothing lacking, for the building will be constr~ on the most up-to-date lines and will affbrd every reasonable facility for that solid grounding in education which is so essential to the rising generation. The Mayor ventured the opinion that the school would be one of the cheapest in the country, but there is no reason to fear that it will be the worse on that account. The prospect for the ratepayer is not altogether cheerful, for Mr. R. T. Fairclough, the Chairman of the Sites and Buildings Oommittee, predicted that a new school would be required each year to cone efficiently with the ever-increasing needs of the community.
resist the application for the Provisional Order until they came to terms on the other matters. The resolution was approved. EVENING SCHOOLS. _

The meeting then resolved itself into a meeting of the Parish Council with Mr. E. Bradshaw as clerk. Mr. Clarke reported that it had been decided to hold evening classes during the coming winter in the follow- ing subjects :—Commercial correspondence and business methods type-writing and book-keeping, commercial arithmetic, shorthand, dressmaking, cookery and ambulance. Mr. Rose had again been appointed corres- pondent.

THE PROPOSED RECREATION GROUND. The committee appointed to consider the question of the obtaining of land for the purposes of a recreation ground, reported that they had an offer before them in respect to land off Fairfield-road. Before making any final settlements however they desired to meet the Latchford Without Parish Council to see if that authority would join them in the scheme. Mr. Hallows: Is it.going to be a park or a play, ground for the children. If it is to be a park you are going to get the united opposition of the parish. Mr. Bouchier suggested that it would be better for them to acquire the land before deciding what to do with it. Land was rapidly being built upon and unless they acquired a plot at once they would probably lose the chance of doing so. Mr. Brown: I take it it will be a place where people can go to rest. If it is going to be a play ground for football and such games I oppose it altogether. The matter was then allowed to drop, pending an interview with the Latchford Council. It will be again introduced in September and will later be laid before the half-yearly parish meeting.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH AND ELECTRIC
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH AND ELECTRIC
LIGHT. -- Opposition to Corporation Proposals.
PROPOSED RECREATION GROUND.

The lighting of Stockton Heath was the principal business under discussion at Tuesday night's meeting of the Parochial Committee of that village. Mr. G. Pilling presided and there were present :—Messrs. J. W. Bouchier, F. Pearson, G. J. Brown, J. H. Clarke, J. Whitley, T. R. Westbrook, H. J. Westbrook, J. Hallows, J. McDermid, G. F. Ashton (clerk), and J. Swinton (surveyor). At a previous meeting of the Committee the Lighting Committee was instructed to report upon the cost of lighting the village with electricity, but no report was presented on Tuesday. Referring to the question, Mr., H. J. Westbrook, said he saw in one of the Warrington papers that Stockton Heath having made a request to the Corpora- tion of Warrington to supply electric light, the Corpor- ation proposed applying for a Provisional Order for the supply of electricity in the district. He understood that the intention of the Committee was that the village should be lit from the existing electric mains. Mr. Whitley explained that he had waited on the Electricity Committee of the Corporation with the object of ascertaining at what cost the Committee would light Stockton Heath with electricity. What had appeared in the papers had, he thought, arisen out of that visit. Mr. Browne said the Electricity Committee had agreed to send in prices if Stockton Heath would forward a requisition. What appeared on the minutes of the Council was incorrect. Stockton Heath had no inten- tion of making any such requisition and if the Corpora- tion refused to give an estimate in a proper businesslike manner he took it that the thing was at an end. Mr. Bouchier explained that he had seen a Corporation official and asked him to lay the prices of electric light before the Parochial Committee.' He gave that gentleman to understand that Stockton Heath would not for a moment consider the question of the Cor- poration applying for powers because they were not going to give anyone a monopoly. Mr. H. J. Westbrook moved: "That this comitittee having read that it has been reported that in conse- quence of Stockton Heath having made a requisition the Corporation intend to apply for provisional order to supply the district with electricity, hereby records that such report is absolutely incorrect and unfounded." Without expressing any opinion as to whether the Corporation should have the order or not he thought the Parochial Committee should have a look in and see that they got value for their money. Mr. Clarke seconded. They had a grievance against the Corporatiou in the price the village was charged for gas, and also in regard to the imposition of the extra tram fare. The Corporation obtained power to enter the village with gas long before the Parochial Committee was in existence. The Parochial Cotuinittee was in existence when the Corporation moved in the matter of the tramways, and, subject to certain terms, agreed to the tramway entering the village. They all knew the treatment which they had received. A promi- nent official made a distinct promise that the fare should be a certain amount, and that promise bad never been carried out. If the Corporation secured the pro- posed Order,they would have a very valuable monopoly, and they wanted Stockton Heath to he like a fly and respond to their request to fall into the trap by sending in a requisition. Until the existing grievances were removed he would not consent to the granting of any further monopoly to the Corporation,and would strongly

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
The latest " agony" reads : "To Summer Come back and all will be forgiven."

* * - From America the story comes that two proposals of marriage took place recently in a submarine at the bottom of Lake Ronkonkoma, Long Island. Heavily handicapped as they were the ladies naturally accepted the -proposals, but it strikes us as being rather a "low down" trick on the part of the two swains.

The father of Mr. Sherwell, the South African Captain, lives in England, and he promised his son a sovereign for every run he made in last week's test match. Shervrell's great score of 115 in the second _innings will not be forgotten for a long time by cricket enthusiasts, and for him it must have doubly pleasant recollections, for he was presented with a handsome cheque by a proud father on Tuesday.

* * * Commenting on Mr. Winston Churchill, M.P., in " P.T.0.," Mr. T. P. O'Connor says :—I regard the son as a far more brilliantly and largely endowed being than even the very remarkable father. Winston has wider and better education, a more copious vocabu- lary, greater concentration of purpose, than his parent. He can say of himself what Napoleon always used to say: "lam above all things, un homme 41e politique." _

* * The Marquis of Cholmondeley, who celebrated his birthday on Wednesday, is, although Lord Great Chamberlain of England', a man of simple tastes, who prefers the life of a country squire. Cholmondeley Castle, his Cheshire seat, contains some beautiful Dutch tapestry and pictures by Vandyck and Rubens, as well as a magnificent gold tea and coffee service, which once belonged to George Fourth. In one of the reception-rooms may be seen the declarations against transubstantiation made by the late Queen and by King Edivaid

* * * The Jarrow election result was hardly a surprise, and not a very great disappointment to Liberals. We should certainly have liked to see Mr. Hughes win the seat, if only for those qualities of humour which have made him one of the most popular journalists of the day. "Sub Rosa "will have to bide his time, and try again when the political sea is less choppy than it as at Jqrrow. Mr. Pete Curran, M.P., is a good type of Labour representative, and there is no doubt that his plucky fight in 1906 had much to do with the workers pinning their faith to him once more. _ _

_ The. fact that the Member for Warrington made his maiden speech last week reminds us that Mr. Crosfield's record compares favourably with that of any of his predecessors. A great many members of the House of Commons never speak at all, and the late Mr. McMinnies, though the most popnlar public speaker Warrington ever knew, never addressed the House. The late Sir Gilbert Greenall spoke on one occasion only during the long time in which he represetnted Warrington, and if we are not mistaken the tenour of his speech was to suggest that a certain window be either closed or opened. Mr. R. Pierpoint spoke on more than one occasion, but his remarks were always confined to the Island of Cyprus, in which he took an inordinate interest. Mr. Crosfield is the only Warrington Member who has genuinely intervened in serious debate and given the Members of the House his views on a matter of national importance. More power to him!

- - While in London, Mr. Crosfield has been keeping in close touch with both Liberal and Labour members. The member and his accomplished sister, Miss Oros- field, have been giving a- series of—shall we say —politico-social dinners. Some weeks ago they had the privilege of entertaining, in company with Mr. and Mrs. Charles E, Parker, a party or-Labour mem- bers including the Bight. Hon. John Burns, Mr. Fen- wick, Mr. Maddison, Mr. Shackleton, and Mr. H. Vivian. Mr. Crooks and Mr. Walsh were present at a subsequent gathering. Some time ago Mr. Crosfield and his sister had the honour of giving a large party for the Prime Minister, and about a week ago they gave a dinner party to Mr. and Mrs. L Harcourt, Mr. and Mrs. Pease, Mr. Lloyd George, and Mr. McKenna. The member for Warrington ought to be well- informed on political matters! He is devoting much time and trouble to Parliamentary and other duties inseparable from his position, and is, we are glad to say, in better health than formerly. * *

The speech-making at the Training College prize distribution on Saturday was not without its amusing touches. Canon Stevenson, the genial principal, disclaimed all intention of saying anything humorous, giving as an excuse the general depression caused by the miserable weather which had interfered with several College functions and threatened to spoil some of the recreations of that day, which included dancing on the lawn. Bishop Welldon, who dis- tributed the prizes, caused , great laughter by remarking that the Principal's speech had, after all, not lacked humour especially when he said they had been asked there for the purpose of dancing on the lawn and looked at him (the Bishop) for,be it understood, Bishop Welldon is a very portly gentle- man and the idea of his "tripping the light fantastic , toe " quite tickled the assembly. His lordship hastened to assure them that that was not the purpose for which , he had come to Warrington, but gallantly concluded,: "I will proceed to choose my partner when I can make a proper discrimination between the candidates for my hand." . .

* * * An amusing anecdote of the late Mr. Gladstone was told by Colonel Darbishire at the opening of a convalescent home at Penmaenmawr, one of the great statesman's favourite resorts. Once when the Grand Old Man was staying at Penmaenmawr there was to be an autumn session, when Mr. Marriott's amend- ment --a famous Parliamentary occasion—had to be dealt with. There was also staying at Penmaenmawr the Solicitor General for Ireland, Mr. Gibson, who was on the other side of the House. These gentlemen were seen walking together on :he Promenade, and the visitors whispered together, "Now Mr. Marriott's amendment is being settled." "But," said Colonel Darbishire, " my eldest son, then a little fellow, and who was an illustration of the proverb Little pitchers have long ears,' had been playing near where the great men were conversing, and he said, e They were not talking about Mr. Marriott's amendment. What I heard Mr. Gladstone say wAs 'I do not find the bathing of this place quite so interesting as on the Continent, because the ladies wear such ugly bathing dresses."-4-(Loud laughter.)
