div.head: BOLTON SCHOOL.
div.p: THE BOLTON SCHOOL.
LAYING OF THE MEMORIAL STONE

Yesterday afternoon the Mayor( Alderman Smethurst) laid the memorial stone of the Bolton Council school which is being erected in Lower Wash-lane to meet the requirements of the Latchford district. The school will consist of two departments, viz., for girls and infants. The ground floor is to accommodate 360 infants and will be divided into class rooms. The first floor will be arranged to hold 360 girl scholars and the number of class rooms will be similar to those on ground floor, but one of the class rooms will be fitted up as a Science room. Each floor will have a lateral hall 50ft. !tins. by 25ft. wiie and the class rooms will open into same; thus the whole of the class rooms will have perfect supervision from the head master. The head teachers' rooms will be placed on the ground and first floors respectively, and those to accommodate the assistant teachers will be placed on the mezzanine floors. The cloak rooms and corridors will be of ample size and width and each floor will have the usual caretaker's ' and book stores. in addition there is to be a cookery class room and entered from the outside for practical and demonstration classe and this department is to be utilized as a centre. There will be a basement under cookery department with the usual offices I and stores and a large kitchen to be used if necessary for meals. The scheme provides for a caretaker's house with parlour, kitchen and scullery, with the usual out-offices on the ground floor, and three Ibedrooms and bath-room on the first floor. As economy I was made one of the essential features in the erection 'of these buildings the designs are necessarily of a plain and simple character. The outside facings are of grey St. Helens brick with a red pressed brick base and the few dressings are of red terracotta. A strip of the playground 35 feat in width along the whole of the south side adjacent to the new street is to be laid out as a garden for the purpose of" Nature Study," and a portion of the playground is to be covered in to use as a playshed and for drilling in wet weather. The buildings are being erected by Mr. Harry Fair- dough, of Warrington, from the designs of J. E. Wright, Garnett and Wright, of Warrington. There was a large gathering to witness yesterday's ceremony and fortunately the weather was fine. Councillor FULTON Surrit (chairman of the Education Committee) presided and said they hoped the future generation would bless that day, because the committee were providing a school which would give them all the advantages which skill and knowledge could bring to bear and would tit them to be good citizens and mem- bers of the Empire. Not only would the development of their minds be considered but physical training, which was equally important, would not be overlooked. The difficulties of the teachers would also beminimised by the healthy surroundings. The MAYOR then delivered an address in the course of which he said the new school was to take the place I of the Infants' school meeting in Grappenhall-road and partly to replace the Christ Church school in Wash- lane. The Committee had provided sufficient land to allow of a boys' department being erected when required. Three years ago it was felt that the time for this extension was far distant, but the rapid development of this district would make it necessary, before long, for the committee to complete their plans. This school was to cost about £B,OOO and, when completed would probably be one of the cheapest schools in the country. Economy without efficiency was not an advantage, and, from his own knowledge of the schools, and from the information obtained from experts, they knew that the work of their schools was not behind that of any other authority. "I lay this stone" Concluded the Mayor "praying that the Almighty Father of us all may bless the teachers and the children who will work within its walls ; that He will direct them in all their ways ; and that they may be brought to be true citizens, not only of this town, but of His Kingdom." The Mayor was then presented by the architects (Messrs. J. E. Wright, Garnett and Wright) with a handsome silver trowel which had been supplied by Messrs. Eustance and Co. ._ _ _

The CLERK OF THE WORKS (Mr. H. Hallard) handed the Mayor a mallet which, he said, had been turned out of a piece of oak, taken from the farm which stood on that site about 400 years. His WORSHIP then formally laid the stone, after which the Mayor's Chaplain (Rev. W. BRACECAMP) offered prayer. Mr. H. Romvps (deputy-chairman of the Education Committee) moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor. For many years he was associated with his Worship as a member of the Council, and he could say without fear of contradiction that a more energetic, honourable-minded, honest colleague than Alderman Smethurst it would be impossible to have. Mr. Roberts also paid a graceful tribute to the Mayoress. Alderman TrsNroN seconded. He said they would all regret, if when his term of office expired, his Worship did hot see his way to accept it for another year. Alderman Tinnion expressed the hope that the building of schools would soon be made an imperial charge. The vote was heartily accorded. _ .

Canon MORLEY STEVENSON (chairman of the School Management Committee) moved a vote of thanks to Councillor Fulton-Smith. Mr. K. T. FAIRCLOUGH, in seconding, said that in order to keep pace with the town's requirements he thought they would have to build a new school every year. The vote having been accorded, the proceedings closed with the singing of the National" Anthem.

div.head: TRIP DAY.
div.p: TRIP DAY.
WORKS EXCURSIONS FROM WARRINGTON.

Saturday was Warrington's annual trip day and in connection with the various works numerous excursion's to seaside resorts were organised. The result was that the town was almost deserted. On the whole the weather was favourable and the trippers spent a very enjoyable time. _ - -

Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, Ltd. Blackpool was again selected by the employees of the above firm for the annual trip on Saturday. The trippers numbered some 1,800, and were conveyed in trains supplied by the Cheshire Lines Committee. This was the 40th annual excursion, and was as enjoyable as any which have preceded it. The weather was fine. All the usual places of interest were visited, and a very enjoyable day was spent. Mr. William Warburton proved himself an efficient hon. secretary. Some 200 of the visitors took advantge of the extension ticket and prolonged their stay in Blagkpool over the week end.

Richmond's Employees at Dublin. The employees of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Ltd., went much farther afield than usual, Dublin being visited. About 400 workmen accompanied by friends left Warrington for Holyhead at 10.50 on Friday night, the total number being smaller than for previous excursions, owing to the nufavourable weather experienced lately, and in some measure to fear of sea- sickness. The Directors of the Company had made the usual arrangements in regard to the fares of the work- people, and the special train provided was largely made up of saloons. The travelling from Warrington to Holy'llead was done without crowding or discomfort of any kind,and the time passed very pleasantly. At Holy- head the special boat s.s. " Hibernia " was waiting the arrival of the train, and no time was lost by the party in transferring from the train to the boat. The night bbing calm and clear the voyage was much enjoyed and Dublin reached in good time. The breakfast arrangements were carried out most satisfactorily at the Clarence Hotel, immediately after the arrival of the Boat. Mr. John A. Ransoms entertained the heads of the departments and foremen to a substantial meal. Breakfast over many visited Pheonix Park and other sights of interest, but the principal attraction was the Irish International Exhi- bi tion,where the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co.have a fine stand and make a prominent display of their numerous manufactures connected with the gas industry. div.head: VOICE OF LABOUR.
div.p: THE VOICE OF LABOUR.
Edited by John Workman.

Readers of this column are invited to assist in making it interesting and helpful to social workers by contributing themselves. Correspondents must write on one side of the paper Only, and endeavour to make their letters and notes short and to the point. A nom-de-plume may be used, but the real name of the writer should be forwarded in confidence to the Editor of the column. M.S.S. must be addressed to John Workman, " Examiner " Office Warrington and should be sent in not later than Wednesday in each week.
Curran (Lab.)' 4698 Rose-Tunes (U.) Hughes (L.) 3474 O'Hanlan (Nat.)

1 Socialist and Labour majority 768 The result of the poll at Jarrow is inspiriting to Social and Labour adherents. Never before has the constituency been represeated by any other but a Liberal. The change has come after 22 years of Liberalism in a remarkable way. The Socialist or Labour M.P. has beaten all comers—the kTories, Liberals and Nationalists. I congratulate him very heartily on his victory, and wish him good health so that he may continue to fight the people's cause. There are several matters of interest arising out of the Election. ilociever, Ido not intend to offer any criticism. Socialism his won, and I am delighted with the result.

I am very sensible that the position I occupy as Editor .of this column will engage me in careful and formal inquiry into the various discussions which perplex the minds of my readers. My chief desire is to see fair-play; and to allow each an opportunity of explaining the cause on principle he believes to be of importance to the social and political well-being. I have tried to keep the contributions within bounds but I am afraid the column we were promised when we set out has been Often exceeded ; in fact, on one occasion we ran into several columns of the space reserved for Correspondence. For that concession, our thanks are due to the Editor of the Examiner.

Mr. C. E2Parker in his answer to Ur. Quelch makes several observations and inquiries to which doubtless the Editor of Justice will reply effectively. With the personal issue I have no concern. He raises, however, several points which are of consider- able interest to Socialists. Crowded as his letter is with personal judgments and unique tracings of germinal ideas, one cannot fail to see the Parkerian style of diction. That is not all, though. It seems to me that he is guilty of onr-emphasizing the agreement" to take a leap in the dark"; and he exaggerates the arrogance of Socialists. Certainly, it is an unusual experience to road over his signature a letter so lacking in liberal indications of genuine faith in humanity, and so uncharitable in its conclusions.

I c,annot-titink that party bias has warped his views. And yet there is something unaccountable in the pessimistic and uncharitable views he presents to us. I understand that Mr. Parker is " somewhat " of a Socialist. He is a progressive. What he cannot make out is—and on this seems to depend his avowal of the cause—on what system work is to be paid for under Socialism.

Now it is not altogether a wholesome occupation to be always looking into one's intellectual stomach. If you remember the parable of the labourers in the Vineyard, Jesus Christ there taught a lesson which I think showed on what system work is to be paid for. Each man received according to his needs. Each man worked to supply numan needs. Socialism aims at satisfying in the resultant the individual needs of the contributors.

. I would commend Mr. Parker to the remarks of Mrs. Robert Garnett. Speaking at the opening of the new works and tower of Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, she is reported to have said that "she also trusted that the firm did not exist merely to make money, but that they were looking forward with Rudyard Kipling to the time " When no man should work for ,noney or fame, but all for the joy of working." That would be a glorious time, but they must look forward to it, and have high ideals, or they would never carry them out." I admire her enthusiasm, and it is prodigiously elevating. Bat how is such a state to be brought about? Can it come tbrough the present competitive system ? Mr. Parker chastises Socialists for venturing t, speak for the whole working class. If I wished to retaliate I should ask him-why he audaciously claims to speak for the Country? "The Country," he says, " is getting tired of the reiteration of the statement about nationalising the means of production." That is not only a preposterous statement, but it is incor- rect. What authority has Mr. Parker to speak for the country? He, himself, believes that all the natural elements should be nationalized. The nationalization of the means of production is a natural and logical sequence. Many men employed to-day are ceasing_to be looked upon as men; they are simply so much producing power. That is a statement of fact. It used to be lawful to buy and sell men and women; to-day we buy and sell their heart-beats only. Now, if it is wrong to 'buy the whole man is it not wrong to buy or sell part of a man? I believe lam correct when I say that labour can be bought and sold regardless of the man behind it. Under the formulas of supply and:demand,backs bent or hearts broken do not count. If lablur is a com- modity then that doctrine gives man property in man. The great fundamental principle of anti-slavery is that man cannot hold property in man. How do you, therefore, reconcile the statement that the majority of the workers in the country do not consider themselves "slaves" and have no faith in the Socialist remedy? But you want to know on what system work is to be paid for, and until you know, Capitalism is to continue to count into its purse the ruddy drops from morn till noon, from noon to dewy eve, the while stifling its conscience by the thought, "I know not whence they came, or how." I sometimes wonder how we Christian folks have the faith we profess. We believe in the hereafter, bet we will not reconcile the present with the teachings of Christ. We profess the brotherhood of man and the fatherhood of God so long as we are not asked to share each other's burden. Can we wonder that the masses are outside the churches? A little more practical christianity, a little more 'faith in humanity, a little more love, and the Church would come into her own. How long is Christianity to be the tool of money makers? "When there are no more memories of heroes and martyrs. And when all life and all the souls of men and women are discharged from any part of the earth, Then only shal liberty or the idea of liberty be discharged from that part of the earth, And the infidel come into full possession." Wearied with its vain efforts to find happiness in money-making, mankind is now returning to its older and wiser self, and is seeking to find in service that content and peace of mind which selfishness has failed to give. So mote it be. I have been frequently asted for the Basis of the Fabian Society. It is as follows :

div.head: WHITECROSS V. ST. JOHN'S.
div.p: WHITECROSS V. ST. JOHN'S.

The annual report of the Medical Officer of Health has just been presented to our local Council, and contains some very striking figures, remarks and criticisms. The report ought to be read and weighed carefully by all and sundry who take an interest in. the welfare of our "good old town." Judged, how- ever, from a medical point of view the " old town is not good in its older parts, as is poiatedly evidenced by the startling facts referred to in the report. Com- pare Whiteeross Ward with St. John's Ward. Whitecross and St. John's are both largely working class Wards, but the workers in Whitecross are said to be in regular employment, and mostly in receipt of good wages as things go. St John's Ward has a population chiefly composed of laboure..s and others whose means of livelihood are somewhat precarious. Whitecross is of modern date with a fair space between the rows of houses. St. John's contains very bad slums, courts, alleys, and miserable yards. Soma houses in St. John's have no back door. The children: of St. John's have no playgronnd,except the school yard and the streets. The children of Whitecruss have. many little playgrounds of a sort, yet they serve. Is not this an occasion for the use of the " deadly parallel "beloved of the budding journalist? In the one Ward —regular employment, good wages, decent houses reasonable breathing space. In the other— irregular employment, poor wages, insanitary old houses, human beings crowded together like maggots in a cheese.

What are the results of this difference of conditions? Measured in terms of life they are as follow: Whitecross hay the highly creditable birth rate of 37. St. John's has nearly the same, 34. The pro- duction of human life is practically the same. But Ithe destruction of human life, "Oh, what a falling off was there." The death rate for Whitecross is 12.8. For St. John's it is 20.9 i.e nearly double, the highest death rate (except one) of any Ward in the town. .The death rate from epidemic diseases and from lung diseases is practically double that of Whitecross Ward. The loss of infant life is the same proportion and is absolutely the highest by 26- per 1,000 births than any other Ward. Is it any wonder then that labour men strive for better material conditions of life? Is there any justification for the cheap sneer of the comfortable classes at the mere bread and butter and housing side of the labour campaign? The veriest amateur gardener knows that soil and situation are potent factors if his garden is to produce bloom and fruit for labour spent. Shall the flowers of humanity haveless forethought and attention? The wild, untameable poet has told us that God :has fed one rose with the dust of many men, but we dreamers of dreams and seers of visions have enough imagination to conceive of a time when the fruits of the earth in all t eir manifold splendour and variety shall be utilised for the maintenance and comfort of human life of the best type. That day will be long , a'dawning, however, if the workers of the world wait for the idlers and the parasites to bring it about. IWealth to the producer and those dependent on him ,is the watchword of our embattled line, the motto on diir world wide banner.
LAZARUS.

div.head: GARDEN SUBURBS.
div.p: GARDEN SUBURBS.
Progress of the Warrington Scheme.
LAND SECURED AT SANKEY AND GRAPPENHALL.

The Warrington Garden Suburbs Ltd., have decured in addition to the twenty acre plot in the Liverpool- road, a second piece upon Which it is intended to develop a garden suburb. This land is twenty-two acres in extent, and is known as the Morris Brook Farm. It stands on the south side of the Ship Canal, near the locks, and is opposite Messrs. Richmond's new works.

By securing land on different sides of the town the promoters desire to serve the needs and secure the co-operation of all who desire to take part in the work of improOng the housing conditions of the workers of the Borough. The land acquired by the Suburbs Company to the west of the town is a triangular piece of 20 acres formed by the Liverpool and Penketh roads on the north and south, and bounded on the west by a stream which divides the parishes of Penketh and Great Sankey. It is about ten minutes walk from the Sankey Bridges tram terminus, and equal distance from the Sankey Bridges and Sankey railway stations. It is intended to restrict the number of houses to twelve to the acre as a maximum, and to reserve a substantial portion of the land for recreative purposes. A suggested plan for the -laying out of the land is before us and shows that the estate, if carried out as indicated, will be worthy of the name of Garden Suburb. The Garden Suburbs Company intend to lease building plots to societies,pr individuals who will agree in the leases to conform to the regulations necessary to insure that any house built, or garden laid out, will by their style and character conform to the main prin- ciples for which the Company is formed. A Garden Tenants' Society is already coptemplatod by a number of workinamen on the lines of the suc- cessful Societies already in existence in Ealing and Garden City.

We unde'rstand that the members of the Warrington Co-operative Society are interesting themselves in the matter, and considering whether or no they will take a substantit interest in the undertaking. The Pros- pectus of the Parent Company is in course of prepara- tion, and shares will be offered to the public during the next week or two. The distinctive feature of the Company is the limitation of the dividend to five per cent. Anything earned above this goes to further the development of the undertaking. We understand that the principle of co-operative build- ings on the above lines is rapidly spreading in the country. Over twenty Societies are already in exist- ence, and we hear of Societies already formed in Manchester, Oldham, Liverpool, and several other places. Warrington is, however, we believe the first town to combine the Garden City with the co-operative ideal, and to definately contemplate a series of suburbs which it is hoped may eventually girdle the town. \ An opportunity is afforded to visit the Garden City, Letchworth on Satunlay July 13th by means of an excursion train which is to be tun in connection with Liverpool, Manchester, and Warrington. This will afford a chance for those who are interested in this movement to see what has been-done at the first Garden City. Full particulars of the trip may be obtained from Mr. C. E. Parker or Alderman Bennett, the secretary of the Warrington C3mpany.

div.head: WARRINGTON CYCLIST'S SUCCESS.
div.p: WARRINGTON CYCLIST'S SUCCESS.
Berry Wins Valuable Challenge Cup.

Warriugton's crack cyclist—C. Berry —achieved a notable triumph at Newtown on Saturday, when he carried off the GO guinea challenge cup offered by the Royal Welk Recreation Seciety, in the three mile scratch race. Like several other prominent cyclists he entered for several races, but reserved himself for the great event of the day. For some reason the holder did not turn out to defend his title, and T. Sherratt, Wigan, winner of the cup in 1904 and 1905 was the general favourite, and it was thought that he would .win the trophy outright. Six riders turned out for the final and at the start H. English, Salford, took the lead, closely followed by Sherratt and Berry. This position was kept up until the last two laps when Sherratt, who was riding a little carelessly, came a cropper. Berry forged to the front but half a lap from home Budge (Salford), glided past him, but ' could not maintain his lead. A dozen yards from the post the two men were level when Berry made a great , effort and crossed the tape a length ahead. Time, 10min. 10 3-ssec. Interviewed after the race Berry I said he had been racing for 5 years, his first victory being at Warrington on August Monday, 1902. He I had met Sherratt many times and first defeated him at the Warrington Police Sports in a two-mile race. At Crewe last week he also beat Sherratt. Berry has won , over .41100 in prizes, including twenty firsts. He ! announced his intention, all being well, of again riding Ifor the Cup at Newtown next year.

The National Service League and the Lancashire Sea Training Home for Poor Boys. Sir,—With reference to the announcement recently made by Captain Field that a hammock had been founded in the excellent institution above mentioned, under the name of the National Service League Hammock (Warrington Branch), I think it advisable to make a short statement. In the absence of any informa- tion to the contrary the inference is nl.tural that the Warrington Branch of the League must be exceptionally well in funds to be in a position to devote a sum of £25 per annum in aid of another Society. This is by no means the case. Moreover, even if our Bank balance warranted such a donation our Members would have reason to object to their subscriptions being diverted in favour of another Society when such an immense amount of work still requires to be done done before the Natism is educated s•l'ficiently far to adopt universal training. To come to the point, the hammock in ques- tion is solely due to one of our Members who had this happy idea orassisting both societies at one stroke, the Navy League Home by direct material assistance, the N.S.L. indirectly by advertisement. We recognise and take this occasion to emphasize the value of the work done by the Navy League Training Mime. What it accompliihes for the few fortunate lads who come under its influence is beyond all praise. It is very gratifying to the League that by our friend's generosity we are entitled to show in a practical form our sympathy with a sister association which is ' demonstrating by practical experience how much can be done by a salotary diso:plinP to Iwo-ease the mental and physical fitness of the youth of the nation.—l am fOtlte, etc.,

GEORGE CROSFIELD. Tie Men who Abolished the House of Lords in 1648. fear the present controversies are likely to bring up a great many unpleasant things in history, -which one would be only too glad to allow to rest in oblivion. But thenecessity for meeting certain tactics just now renders it, a matter of duty to remind men once more of the lessons of the past, lessons which it might, have been thought the nation had learnt once for all. The responsibility however for such appeal to history mnst rest with those whose action challenges such appeal. In my former letter on this matter, I drew the attention of your readers to the fact that the people who got rid of the House of Lords, had also got rid of the House of Commons, eot rid also, at least as fares the King was concerned of the administration of jiihtice, getting rid in the end of the King himself. It remains now to show how they also got rid of the people in whose name they professed to act. It will be remembered, certainly by your Irish readers, that soon after the King's execution Cromwell left the Gi.vernment of the country to the tender mercies of the Parliament of 53, together with a Council of State (most of whom were army officers), while he went over to Ireland on his memorable expedition of slaughter. On his return he found the Parliament whom he had allowed to abolish the King and the Lords, theii appetite for power increased by their short exercise of it, seeking to perpetuate their authority in a way that gave him considerable umbrage. The summary way in which he dealt with these gentlemen, whom he simply tie-ned out of the house, is well known. These were *canes in which the people merely occupied the position of passive spectators. The ignoring of the people, however, is more obvious in the next move. Cromwell decided to have a Parliament; for was he not the head of Parliamentary Party? But, it was a Parliament in which the people were not allowed to elect! He nomi- Tilted the members himself with the assistance of his Council of State. A curious lot was this Parliament of 128 members—fifth monarchy men, Anabaptists, Antinotrians, and Independents, a nice assortment of the Free Churchmen of the time. They met and began —so Hume tells us—by "seeking the Lord in Prayer." Cromwell in his usual style told them "that he had never looked to see such a day when Christ should be so owned." These pious gentlemen set to work as they said to pave the way for the Reign of the Redeemer. To that end, us they had already abolished bishops, they now abolished the office of the ministry altogether as savouring of popery. They voted learning heathenish, and the Universities unnecessary. They voted the Common Law a badge of Conquest and of Norman Slavery, and did various other ridiculous things. In the end Cromwell became so sick of the pro- ceedings of this absurd Parliament, to which he had given his blessing, that he managed to get rid of it in -five months. It is not necessary to go through all Cromwell's •experiments in Parliament making, making and unmaking them at his pleasure, and in which the -ordinary reader may be left to judge of his principles of Goverment. It is more to the point to ask how the station and the people fared under such rule. I will give -the answer not in my own words, but in words more authoritative, those of Lord Beaconsfield taken from a letter written by him to Lord Lyndhurst when he was a young man, and which gave a picture of the time which I venture to say is by rio means over-coloured. Be says, speaking of the men who were supreme in these curious Parliaments, in which Parliamentary government was travestied, and the will of the people ignored, but which nevertheless assumed to act for the, people and in their name—be says that" they estab- lished Courts more infamous than-the Star CI-amber in every county of England, with power of fining, seques- trating, imprisoning and corporally punishing all who opposed or even murmured against their decrees; that under the plea of malignancy the People,' as they called themselves, avenged their private hatreds, and seized for then' private greed and gratification any estates or property to which they took a fancy ; that the People' consigned to bastilles and perpetual imprisonment all those who refused to answer their illegal enquiries, and bored red hot irons through the tongues of-the contumacious ; that not an appearance of law or liberty remained in the land; that 'the people' enlarged the laws of high trsason so that they comprehended verbal offences and even inten- tions, that 'the people' practised decimation; they voted trial by jury a breach of Parlia- mentary privilege; they deprived of authority all persons of family and distinction, and filled every office uneer them with the scum of the nation; they -seqaestratecl nearly one half of the goods and chattels of the nation, and at least one half of its rents and revenues: in seven years they raised the taxation of the country from £BOO,OOO per annum to £7,000,000 per annual ; they invented tha excise, and applied that impost even to provisions and the common necessaries of life; they became so barefaced in their vile extor- tions, that one morning they openly divided £300,000 amengst themselvesond settled an annuity of £4 a day -on each of their number." This was the condition to which the country was reduced by the men who -abolished the House of Lords in order that they might have a free hand to govern as they pleased.- E. C. E. CARLETON.
27th June, 1907.

Drink Trade Municipalization. Sir,—The object of all correspondents in the dis- cussion should be to give a true, brief, and lucid exposi- tion of the principles embodied in the subjects. In order to commend our views to the careful considera- tion of the" " mau in the street," we should be most careful to express ourselves in such a manner as to make those views clear and definite to the mind and imagination of those we appeal to. The average man in the street is ever ready to carefully consider sound principles and will eagerly grasp the pith of sound, •sensible argument upon any subjects for the better- ment of the race, but when he sees any party or individual endeavour to force upon him- a -scheme, backed up by no practical experience, with no arguments in its favour, and exposed by those who, when taken to task try shuffle to -out of it by casting sneers and slurs at other individuals and organisations and their principles, he I will not haVe it. It is useless to try and gull the work- ing man with biassed views unless you can convince I him by sound and logical argument. Mr. Stanley Lord was taken up by myself and a highly-respected Good , -Templar friend, Mr. O'Brien. This week your corres- I pondent replies. The first part of his epistle is in reply to Mr. O'Brien, and this he adds" will answer Mr.. Griffiths." Where, I ask, is the answer? He has not brought anything which can refute a single argument I introduced. He does not jefer to the" world's greatest men wno have indulged in stimulants,' nor the "sweetest •singers," previously referred to. He has not attempted ; to "prove that the drink has, in any degree, contributed -to the greatness of any nation." He does attempt to explain the attitude of the Labour party at the tiecond reading of the Scottish Local Veto Bill, and the Local Option majorities at trade union gatherings. Neither does he prove that under Municipalization "it would be, impossible to get drunk." I had almost forgotten that Mr. Lord promised to 'enlarge upon this idea "on the 22nd ult. I looked , for it in vain. Instead of enlarging, be has belittled ' his proposal. For he fails to bring an argument in its favour. He says " It is probable that all serious minded 1 people who desire the well-being of the nation, the 1 improvement of the race are agreed as to the evils of I the present methods of drink distribution." Here ho makes a fatal mistake. The average licence-holder may be as good a man as any Socialist, and they have no right whatever to cast a bad reflection upon his character. While Ido not favour them in any way, I say that they do their best to conduct their houses in a -proper manner and try to manage a businesa which in the hands of others may prove unmanageable. The license holder must act in accordance with strict law end police supervision, and while the tied house has its failures, there are very few "serious minded people" who find fault with the " present methods of drink distribution." The evils we are agreed unon are in the drink itself. It Ratters not to me who the retailer may be. There :are few cases to be found in which the young man has

Prendergast, —a bricksetter's labourer, of Liverpool, employed at the Winwick Asylum, was charged with wounding George William Beard, licensee of the Swan Hotel, Winwick. On Tuesday last week Mr. Beard, hearing a noise in the lavatory, found prisoner there, who immediately rushed at him with an open knife and struck him several times in the arm, inflicting a slight wound.—Police-constable Woolfe came on the scene, and prisoner was arrested. Prisoner had pre- viously threatened Mr. Beard, and in the presence of the officer he remarked "Had it not been for you I would have cut his heart out."—Prendergast was committed to the Liverpool Assizes.

at WarringtOn on Tuesday on the body of Patrick Tavian, aged forty-two, a general labourer, who lodged at Hill-street, and who was found dead in bed on Saturday morning. Mary Govan, with whom the deceased lodged, stated that the deceased went to bed at ten minutes to eleven on Friday night under the influence of drink, taking upstairs with him a quart of beer and a small bottle of whisky. This was his usual habit for some time past. The next morning he was found dead in bed with his clothes on, by his landlady. Since he had received compensation for the loss of an eye he had not worked, and had been drinking heavily for some time. Dr. Smith, police surgeon' certified that death was apparently caused through excessive drinking, and the jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence. Wycliffe P.S.A. The attendance at the meeting of the Wycliffe Society on Sunday was small owing to , the holidays. Mr. A. Healey presided and spoke upon the " Mercies of God." Mr. F. J. Adcock, of Manchester, gave an address on "The common people heard Him gladly." He said that the words Christ uttered' went to his hearers with power, inspiring and influencing them to holy and consecrated work. His words and teachings still lived, and guided the work of the Christian Church. Mr. Meachin read the lesson, and Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ and also rendered an organ solo. The Secretary moved a vote of sympathy with one of the members, whose father lost his life in a well at Penketh a few days ago. The resolution was seconded and carried in silence. Fowl-Stealers Punished. Three Warrington men named Adam Thompson, William Thompson, and Thomas Jackson, all residing in Pierpoint-street, were charged before the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) at the Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, with stealing thirty-three tame fowls, value £4 2s. 6d., the property of Councillor Dickinson, Froghall Bridge. Inquiries were made by the police, and the prisoners were arrested early that morning by Detective Meacock and P.C. Sankey, and they then admitted their guilt. John Gibson, of Pierpoint-street, pleaded guilty to receiving the fowls knowing them to have heel\ stolen. —The Mayor said it was a serious offence,and Oriso-ers would have to go to gaol for six weeks each with hard labour. "LEA-FRANCIS," "PREMIER," and " BUDGE- WHITWORTH" CYCLES. Price from £4 10s. Cash or easy payments.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Warrington Chess Club. Members of the Warrington Chess Club held their annual gathering at Atkinson's Cafe on Thursday evening. The president, Mr. E. L. Fleming presided and there were present :—Measrs. J. R. Wood, T. A. Sutton, J. Newcombe, 0.1. Cooke, W. H. Bell, W. Johnston, C. Johnstone,W. Warburton, F. Warburton, C. A. Littler, W. J. Barnes, E. L. Fleming, F. Dunne, J. Rathbone and E. England. Letters of regret for non-attendance were received from Messrs. Z. Armitage, McDonald, R. Ockel, Taylor, Greening,l Fairhurst, 41dritt, Connolly, Wood, H. Bond, , Chambers and Warren. Much interest was aroused by reason of the finalists for the championship trophy, Messrs. F. Warburton and W. H. Bell having drawn two games whilst one was unfinished. It was decided that one hour's play should be allowed in the, third game, and it being still unfinished at the expiration of that period, the match was awarded by the Committee to Mr. Warburton. Later the presi- dent handed the Silver King to the winner. It was a rather remarkable coincidence that the winner of the championship in 1906 was Mr. Warburton's brother. The ordinary business of the annual meeting was then proceeded with. The balance sheet, which was unanimously approved showed that the year closed with a small balance in hand The president and secretary (Mr. J. R. Wood) were unanimously re-elected. Messrs. E. L. Fleming, J. R. Wood, F. Warburton, H. Bond, F. Dunne, A. Wood, W. H. Bell, T. A. Sutton, E. England and W. Johnstone and the Rev. C. Harvey-Cook, were elected to form the Com- mittee. Mr. F. Warburton was appointed captain. It was decided to hold the first meeting of the next season on August 22nd. Local Eisteddfod Successes. The Warrington Male Voice Choir secured a notable victory at Newtown (Montgomeryshire) musical festival on Saturday, being awarded the first prize of £3O with a three guinea medal to the conductor (Mr. S. Hassell). Eleven choirs had entered for the com- petition but Cilfynydd, Newport (Mon) and Towyn did not appear. Warrington Apollo were disqualified because they did not come in time-32 of their 'Am- bers had arrived, but waited for the absent twelve, who came in by the afternoon train—but fortune willed that they should be drawn to sing first. The other choirs sang in the following order: —Abergorky, Oceanic (Cwmparc),Birmingham Victoria,Macbyulleth, Mvelwyn, Warrington, Mountain Ash.. Dr. W. G. McNaught wee the adjudicator and the test piece was "The destruction of Gaza" (De Rifle). In commenting upon the Warrington choir's performance,Dr.McNaught said the pianoforte was so slightly and delicately touched that it might have been non-existent. It was quite unnecessary -for this choir to have a single tip from the piano. There was some real culture in the style, and a smooth musical tone. There was real unity; the Choir was welded together. There was a mood in the opening, some breath, some ringing, and a clean finish. The Choir had a beautiful blend, was ' tuneful, sweet, expressive, and they seemed all desirous of getting at the heart of the piece. The allegro was very good, not to fast ' • the last movement was very good indeed. The attack was spirited and very '.exact. He awarded them 72 marks. The second prize of SAO went to , Moelwyn. In the brass band contest (test piece "II Trovatore ") the first prize was awarded to Goodshaw, I she second to Irwell Springs, and the third to Cros- fields, and the fourth and fifth prizes were divided between Lindley and Linthwaite. Mr. Angus Holdeni' adjudicated. Only one point divided the first and. second, and Crosfield's came very close behind.

Sir,—lt appears very curious that when we attempt to make ourselves perfectly clear we ofttimes fail to achieve our object. I suppose it is the little we leave unsaid creates the difficulty. Mr. Stanley Lord made a direct appeal to the 1.0.G.T. to join the fray, and I occupied a considerable portion of your space in point- ing out the varied shades of thought in politics and religion from which that body was being constantly and continually recruited to assure him and also, who- ever else may take interest in and read his letters, that whatever attitude or action might be taken by that body. could only be done after considerable deliberation and discussion, from the most energetic Socialist to the more cautions Conserv- ative. I considered it sufficiently germane to the ques- tion to assume that however hostile their ultimate attitude may be to the policy he advocates, it is at least worthy of respect as the result of thoughtful con- viction and not wild enthusiasm, and I also feel that the word "fanatic" is and has been too frequently used by the unthinking against those whose views and convic- tions they did not understand. How many times have I heard it applied to some of the ablest thinkers of the Socialistic school by men who never did a half-hour's solid thinking in their lives. It was not worthy a place in such a letter. Mr. Stanley Lord will also notice in support of my opening explanation, that however Mr. Griffiths or myself may differ in our expressions or opinions, we both unhesitatingly agree in our opposition to the adoption of th. above policy. I did not think I had quarrelled with him describing Socialists as sensible. I could not, hut I suggested the quality was not absolutely confined to them. Because I object to being a shareholder in a business I am opposed to Mr. Stanley Lord points out that as a citizen to-day 1. benefit by the revenues of the drink trade. May I point out as a Citizen I have had no hand in bringing about the creation of those revenues and they come to me just the same as the obligations of 1 the rates. lam doing my best according to my light to limit both. • But that does not justify me in taking part in the creation, or allowing the creation without pro- test of another monopoly, in which I shall have a direot interest and a business to which I have an objection. And with the 1.0.G.r. I shall do all I can legitmately, by vote and voice to prevent the adoption of that policy. Should it however by the will of the people become the law, then I like many others, tvho may consider themselves suffering under present unjust laws, would have to submit to the opinion of the majority, and work as hard as I could to effect a change and a repeal ; and this just brines me to another point of difference, I assume that the Social supervision would not prevent drunkenness. Human nature is pretty weak, and I am not quite satisfied that the "benefit of the revenues" would not largely loom up, and would create a disposition to wink at the increase of the drinking for the uses that might be made with the revenue. I imagined Mr. Stanley Lord a young man by the impetuous way in which he attacked the Temper- ance people generally in his letter, but if he considers it an impertinence, I can assure him it is a qualification hundreds would like to possess. But he was rather unkind to suggest that because I confessed to 30 years of Good Templary, I was consequently old and out of date. That is really worse than the "too old at forty,"cry which I am satisfied will not be seriously subscribed to by himself or the Socialists generally, no matter how much we may differ.—l am, yours very truly, PATRICK O'BRIEN.

div.head: Opposition to Corporation Proposals. 'PROPOSED RECREATION GROUND.
div.p: Opposition to Corporation Proposals. 'PROPOSED RECREATION GROUND.

The lighting of Stockton Heath was the principal business under discussion at Tuesday night's meeting of the Parochial Committee of that village. Mr. G. Pilling presided and there were present :—Messrs. J. W. Bouchier, F. Pearson, G. J. Brown, J. H. Clarke, J. Whitley, T. R. Westbrook, H. J. Westbrook, J. Hallows, J. McDermid, G. F. Ashton (clerk), and J. Swinton (surveyor). At a previous meeting of the Committee the Lighting Committee was instructed to report upon the cost of lighting the village with electricity, but no report was presented on Tuesday. Referring to the question, Mr.' H. J. Westbrook, said he saw in one of the Warrington papers that Stockton Heath having made a request to the Corpora- tion of Warrington to supply electric light, the Corpor- ation proposed applying for a Provisional Order for the supply of electricity in the district. He understood that the intention of the Committee was that the village should be lit from the existing electric mains. Mr. Whitley explained that he had waited on the Electricity Committee of the Corporation with the object of ascertaining at what cost the Committee would light Stockton Heath with electricity. What had appeared in the papers had, he thought, arisen out of that visit.

Mr. Bro wne said the Electricity Committee had agreed to send in prices if Stockton Heath would forward a requisition. What appeared on the minutes pf the Council was incorrect. Stockton Heath had no inten- tion of making any such requisition and if the Corpora- tion refused to give an estimate in a proper businesslike manner he took it that the thing was at an end. Mr. Bouchier explained that he had seen a Corporation official and asked him to lay the prices of electric light before the Parochial Committee. He cave that gentleman to understand that Stockton Heath would not for a moment consider the question of the Cor- poration applying for powers because they were not going to give anyone a monopoly. Mr. H. J. Westbrook moved: • That this committee having read that it has been reported that in conse- quence of Stockton Heath having made a requisition the Corporation intend to apply for provisional order to supply the district with electricity, hereby records that such report is absolutely incorrect and unfounded." Without expressing any opinion as to whether the Corporation should have the order or not he thought the Parochial Committee should have a look in and see that they got value for their money. Mr. Clarke seconded. They had a grievance against the Corporation in the price the village was charged for gas, and also in regard to the imposition of the extra tram fare. The Corporation obtained power to enter the village with gas long before the Parochial Committee was in existence. The Parochial Committee was in existence when the Corporation moved in the matter of the tramways, and, subject to certain terms, agreed te the tramway entering the village. They all knew the treatment which they had received. A promi- nent official made a distinct promise that the fare should be a certain amount, and that promise had never been carried out. If the Corporation secured the pro- posed Order,they would have a very valuable monopoly, and they wanted Stockton Heath to be like a fly and respond to their request to fall into the trap by sending in a requisition. Until the existing grievanc.s were removed he would not consent to the granting of any further monopoly to the Corporation,and would strongly resist the application for the Provisional Order until they came to terms on the other matters. The resolution was approved. EVENING SCHOOLS.
The meeting then resolved itself into a meeting of

the Parish Co-uncil with Mr. E. Bradshaw as clerk. Mr. Clarke reported that it had been decided to hold evening classes during the corning winter in the follow- ing subjects :—Commercial correspondence and business methods, type-writing and book-keeping, commercial arithmetic, shorthand, dressmaking, cookery and ambulance. Mr. Rose had again been appointed corres- pondent.

div.head: PROPOSED RECREATION GROUND.
div.p: THE PROPOSED RECREATION GROUND.

The committee appointed to consider the question of the obtaining of land for the purposes of a recreation ground, reported that they had an offer before them in respect to land off Fairfield-road. Before making any final settlements however they desired to meet the Latchford Without Parish Council to see if that authority would join them in the scheme. Mr. Hallows : Is it going to be a park or a play, ground for the children. If it is to be a park you are going to get the united opposition of the parish. Mr. Bouchier suggested that it would be better for them to acquire the land before deciding what to do with it. Land was rapidly being built upon and unless they acquired a plot at once they would probably lose the chance of doing so. Mr. Brown: I take it it will be a place where people can go to rest. /If it is going to be a play ground for football and such games I oppose it altogether. The matter was then allowed to drop, pending an interview with the Latchford Council. It will be again introduced in September and will later be laid before the half-yearly parish meeting.

div.head: NEW CHIEF CONSTABLE.
div.p: NEW CHIEF CONSTABLE.
Mr. Nicholls Welcomed to Warrington.

On Monday Mr. Martin Nicholls entered upon his duties as Chief Constable of Warrington and received a cordial welcome. Before the business of the Police Court opened, The MAYOR said it gave him great pleasure to welcome their new Chief Constable (Mr. Martin Nicholls). He was sure that it was the wish of the whole of the magistrates of the borough, of the neighbouring counties, and of the public at large that Mr. Nicholls should receive a hearty welcome. They trusted that by the blessing of God he and his wife and family would have health and strength to spend a long and happy life in Warrington. The CHIEF CONSTABLE said he was much touched by the kind words the Mayor had addressed to him on his first appearance in that Court. He felt quite unable to say to them what he would like to say, but he would promise one and all that he would use every possible endeavour to give in the discharge of his duties that thorough and entire satisfaction to which the borough was entitled. Mr. BRONVNE said that, on behalf of the splicitors practising in the Court, he wished to be allowed to extend to Mr. Nicholls their heartiest welcome, and to remind the Court that it seemed but yesterday since they welcomed Mr. Talbot, although 12 years had passsd away. He hoped they would have a wotthy successor to Mr. Talbot in Mr. Nicholls. They could , only hope that the advocates would get otiNts well with I him as they did with the late Chief.

ADDRESS TO THE FORCE. At the conclusion of the business of the Court, the police force mustered at full strength in the parade room to be addressed by the new Chief Constable. Many of the magistrates were present. The MAYOR, in formally introducing the Chief Con- stable to the men, said he hoped the latter would work as well as they had , done in the past, and then Mr. Nicholls would have no cause of complaint. He hoped all the men would rely upon the Chief Constable for assistance and direction. The CHIEF CONSTABLE, in reply, said that, as all the men were aware, the Watch Committee had, with the approval of the Council, appointed him their chief officer. At the present moment he had no desire to address the force at any length, but he asked all of them to give him their hearty co-operation and assistance in the work he would be called upon to perform from time to time. He desired that they would not .)nly look upon him as their chief, but also as one to whom they could appeal for help and assistance at any time. He should be willing to help them all he possibly could and he desired, in return, that they would help him to carry out his duties in a satisfactory way so that his work might meet with the approval of the Watch Com- mittee.

jItY DEAR NEPHEWS AND NIECES,— '.O Dear me, how quickly the weeks go round. It seems only yesterday that I was writing my last letter, and now the printer's boy is waiting again to get this into the paper, so that you will not be disappointed. As I sit down to write, I am wondering how many of you have begun the essay I set you last week. I am expecting quite a big response, but, remember, you must not exceed a hundred words. I have a lovely secret for you—what do you think it is? You'll never guess, so I'll tell you. The other day, I bought such a nice big case of Fry's Chocolates, and I intend giving the whole lot away in con- nection with the "Children's Corner," so k€ep an eye on this page every week. I am waiting to hear what you thought of my story, "Peaches and Patches," which ap- peared last week. Have you got any new mem- bers to join the C.C. League yet? Now I must close again. So, "Good-bye.' Ever your affectionate, UNCLE NEI'.

ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDENTS. LEONARD WATSON.—So pleased to have you for a member, and to hear about your new school. DOROTHY TRIVETT.—Thank you very much for your pretty postcard. It has gone right into my album, and looks lovely. ELSIE LEE.—Yes, I am always pleased to hear from any member of the C.C. League. Are you any relation to "Nancy Lee"? Let me know.
CHARLES HARCOURT.—Very well, I•will give you some more puzzles to do shortly. WILD OATS.
They who sow wild oats will reap wild oats. Our young people do not believe this, but it is true, whether it be believed or not.

Boys often begin this sowing at an early age, without any thought of the reaping. They have an idea that it is "spoony" to be " good " ; that it is "soft" to be careful to keep clear of all that is wrong; that it is manly to chew, to swear, and to swagger; that it is "smart" to be careless as to what parents and teachers wish. Young men fancy that they are proving their independence by staying away from tie Bible class 'and throwing out doubts about Christi- anity. They pride themselves on being "out of leading-strings," on their ability to choose their own company, and to judge for themselves how they will spend their evenings, and where they will pass their Sabbath. Their noses take an upward curl at the mention of the "pious young men" who hold on to Sunday school and prayer meeting. They have gotten beyond this! Now, in their hearts they know that "the saints" are right and they themselves wrong. They have no idea of going on in the neglect of God and religion all their lives. They ex- pect to have "a good time" while young, and later in life to turn over a new leaf, and to come out all right in the end. They are sow- ing their wild oats. But who is to reap what they are sowing? And what will the harvest be?
"Whatsoever a man soweth that shall he also reap."

Ohara-der is forming. It is formed in youth. Men at thirty and forty are commonly what they were at twenty, only ripened and har- dened; and at twenty they are apt to be what they were at fifteen, only more set. From the quarries that pre dug under Jerusalem a fine creamy limestone is cut that is soft to the knife or chisel when first taken out, but that hardens into solid rock when exposed to the air. So it is with us. In youth we readily take shape under the influences which we in ; in manhood we find our characters are set. We stamp our souls while young apd plastic with the impress that they are to bear in after-life. Good habits in youth give promise of good habits in mature life. Bad habits in youth give promise of bad habits in after-life. Let our young men understand that sowing wild oats in youth means a liarvest of sorrow and sin. Even if repented f, the old seeds are there, to be fought and bewailed as long as life lasts. Better—far better—is it never to sow seeds of evil. No man ever regretted that he began to serve God in his youth.

Sailors live in a lonely world, for months time it may be, and if childless women may be pardoned for petting poodles, Jack may surely '4e excused ter making friends with almost any Creature that will respond to his attentions. No wonder, suggests the Sea Breeze, that on board ship a dog, a goat, a pig, or a parrot is likely to fine a place in the affections of home. less Jack. it _ .0 . _

Dogs are' verhaps the most favoured pets. Admiral E.ans tells of a fini. bull-terrier he had, which was so great a favourite walk the men that they would come to the mast and ask for "shore leave" for Jowler, just as they did for themselves. As a pet the cat does not hold the same place as the dog, for in the traditions of the sea the cat has a rather shady reputation. Yet Mr. Millen, in his "Log of a Sea Waif," gives a pathetic account of the way a kitten soothed his loneliness when, a boy of eleven years, he had his first hard experience of life at sea. There are instances of shipwracked men risk- ing their lives to save the ship's cat; and a few years ago a sailor escaping from the wreck of a barge off Highland Light, Massachusetts, went back to save his pet, and was lost in the at- tempt. In one instance the pet saved themilor. When the steamer Wadwoooj was crushed and sunk in a storm at Port Townsend, the one man on board as ship-keeper was asleep in his bunk. ' The water was already in the cabin when the cat climbed to his bunk and scratched his face, and was knocked into the water for her pains. Again she scratched, and made such outcry that the man waked just in season to escape. _ _

Bears make fine pets, and' goats would be popular at sea if their omnivorous tastes were not such a serious drawback. When Captain Slocum was sailing alone round the world in his little sloop Spray, Governor Sterndale, of St. Helena, gave him a goat, saying that he would be as companionable as a doge But after the first day, ,and as soon as he got his " sea- legs " under him, the goat began eating every- thing aboard ship. The captain tied him up and went about some work forward, but the beast ate himself free from the rope, went into the cabin, and de- voured a fine chart of the West Indies. The n'oxt thing to go was the captain's straw hat, and the beast, after trying to eat everything, from the flying jib to the tiller rope, was 01:111- marily put ashore at the first landing, Ase-sn- sion Island.

Four years ago the sensational papers made much of the fact that a Newport. society wpman carried a little white pig when she made A call. But to find a, pig in Jack's lap would cause no sensation on shipboard. Admiral Evans, when captain of a war-ship, was roused one night to hear the announce- ment that " Dennis " had been found. Dennis, the pet pig, had mysteriously disappeared some days before, having, as it proved, slipped into a coal-bunker. His finding vas deenh2d a matter of sufficient moment to warrant calling the commander at midnight, and Captain Evans rose to see that the ship's cook properly eared for this famished pet. But Dennis finally (F..E.(1 at Fortress Monroe, of eating too many white- oak acorns.

div.head: GIRLS.
div.p: GIRLS.

Girls do not always know their power. It is far greater than they think; and, were they true and brave enough to exert it, they might almost, in a generation, revolutionise society about them. Exert your power for good upon the young men who are privileged to enjoy your society. Gentle and good, be also brave and true. Try to exhibit the ideal of a woman—a pure and good woman—whose life is mighty as well as beautiful in its maidenly dignity and at- tractive loveliness. Do not let it ever seem that dress and frivolity constitute your only thoughts; but let the elevation of your char- acter and the usefulness of your life lift up the man that walks by your side. Some of you are in intimate assodations, which, under ex- changed promises, look forward to a nearer and more enduring relation. In these hours do nothing to lower, but everything to refine and ennoble. each other's character.

Schoolmaster: "Johnny, can you tell me any- thing you have to be thankful for during the past quarter?" Johnny (without hesitation): "Yes, sir." Schoolmaster: " Well, Johnny, what is it?" Johnny: Why, when you broke your arm, you couldn't lick us for two (monthe."

Little Girl (looking over advertising page): "Mamma, why do all these seaside boarding- houses object to children?" Fond Mother: -I` I'm sure I don't know. Go and see what baby is crying about, and tell Johnny to stop throwing things at people in the street, and make George and Kate stop flghting, anfl tell Dick if he doesn't stop blowing that tin trum- pet I'll take it away from him."

div.head: OUTSIDE AD INSIDE
div.p: OUTSIDE AD INSIDE

"Poor little Ida!" " Why, auntie, what are you pitying her for? I don't know of a girl any- where that has so many nice things as she has. I'm sure I should be perfectly happy if I had such beautiful rings, and such a lovely pair of bracelets. You needn't smile at that, auntie, for I know I should; and she has lots of pretty dresses, and her aprons are always stylish. And no end of sashes and hair-ribbons, and that elegant locket and chain—oh, she's always having something new." "Everything that money can buy, I know; but there are some things that money can't buy." "Why, what? I thought money would do everything." "No, little Jenny, money can't buy a pleasant temper and a happy disposition; and I pity Ida be- cause she has neither." tag " Well—yes—l know she does get mad awful easy, and at home the boys like to hector her just to see her 'fly to pieces,' as they say—" "Yes, that's it, and so she is never happy long at a time, for all the fine things you admire so much. If she would not mind the boys' nonsense when they say things on purpose to tease her, they would soon leave off trying it; but she flies into a rage in an instant, and the more angry she gets, the better they enjoy it, and the more they say to keep her going." "I don't think it's right or kind for her brothers to do so." "Of course, it isn't, my dear; but we shall always find plenty of people ready to tease and annoy us if we allow ourselves to be teased, so we must learn not to mind such things." "I've wondered a great many times why Ida didn't seem happier than any other girl, when she has so many things to make her so, but I know she doesn't, and I think the reason must be that she hasn't the ' happy ' inside of her." "You've guessed right. If the ' happy ' isn't inside, all the fine things in the world won't bring it." "Well, auntie, I know I've envied Ida her fine things a great many times, but I believe I never will again. I'll try and keep happy inside, and then I'll be sure of good times always."

Father: "I hear, my b 4, that you are in the habit of telling falsehoods. This grieves me to the heart. Always tell the truth, even though it may bring suffering upon you. Will you promise me?" "Yes, sir." "Very well. Now go and see who is knocking at the door. If it is Bing.ly. say I'm not at home." Conductor: "How old are you, little girl?" Little Girl: "If the company doesn't object, I prefer to pay my fare and keep my own sta- tistics."

The report of Miss Gaffikin, acting medical officer, was presented to the Council. Alderman BENNETT said he would like to refer to two points. The first was the question of infantile mortality. The Dvotor baici ; It must regretfully be recorded that the infant death-rate of Warrington is distressfully high, viz., 157 per 1,000 births, the greatest number of infants deaths occurring in St. John's Ward." There was, said the Alderman, a great element of tragedy underlying these figures, and civilization had by no means said its last word about the question. The Health Committee were no doubt alive to the importance of the question but there was a suggestion he should like to make, and that was that a proper municipal supply of sterilized milk should be made for the use of the infants, so many of whom were sacrificed through want of proper food and other causes. (Hear, hear.) lie would also like to allude to the smoke nuisance. Every year he found his opinion on th 3 sub- Iject was fortified by expert opinion. Dr. Gaffikin, almost needless to say, took the same view of the question as the late Dr. Gornall, and the view also held by every enlightened officer. It must be evident , that smoke must tend not only to the destruction of vegetation, but have a detrimental effect on the public health. That could be proved up to the hilt. It would be idiotic to say he wished to interfere with the industries of the town. He was anxious to see the town thrive, but there was no economy in the way in which smoke was now emitted from , works chimneys. On the contrary the way in I which their manufacturers dealt with the smoke I was extravagant and unsatisfctory. Messsr. Cros- fields had proved this beyond all doubt and by the introduction of modern methods had effected a saving of £25,000 a year. It was absolutely beyond question that the smoke nuisance could be dealt with, with economy to the manufacturers and with enormous advantage to the toilers of the town,and their municipal future would be unsatisfactory and unworthy unless they dealt with the great scourge. He was very sorry indeed that the Sanitary Committee were so little alive to their auty in the matter, and it seemed to him that the only way to rouse themlwould be to take the power from them and put it in the hands of Government inspectors. They were so afraid of offending the manu- factures, so filled with the narrow-minded idea that they might be interfering with local industries, so obsessed with the idea that smoke was so much wealth and riches that they absolutely dared not move in the matter. Alderman TIN-SION said that as Chairman of the Paving and Seweiage Committee he felt it his duty to take exception to the paragraph in the Doctor's report with reference to back streets and passages. He thought Miss Qaffikin must have got the paragraph from ont of an old report of Dr. Gornall's. They had succeeded in convinoing Dr. Gornall of the error of his ways and it was rather unfortunate that they had not brought Miss , Osafikin to the stool of penitence before she fell into I rho fa4ror. Daring the last two years the committee had Ipaved 4i miles of passages and streets. The cost to 4 pv °party owners had been £14,916, and the work in hand lamounted to £4,172.. The applications before the Local Government Board came to £l2, 937 ; in all £32,000 for !private street works. In face of those figures, which did not express pious opinion, he did not think the 1 report should be allowed to pass without a strong pro- test trom the Paving and Sewerage Committee at the Isomewhat reckless and unguarded statements as to the !paving of the streets. Alderman BOLTON said he did not think there was any more smoke in Warrington than anywhere else. If there were no smoky chimneys there would be no money in the pockets of the ratepayers' and Alderman Bennett would not be needed to audit accounts. (Laughter.) Messrs. Crosfield had been quoted, but their case was different to that of the other manufacturers. He (Alderman Bolton) was able t 6 grow orchids and they required the purest air that could be got. Councillor Dr.JosEeH said he did not want to set him- sel f up as an advocate of smoke,but as a matter of fact he was very doubtful as to whether it was not absolutely good for the public health of the town. It contained a very powerful disinfectant against scarlet fever and such 1 diseases. It was a wrong impression that smoke in ! towns was absolutely injurious, because there were many authorities, and good ones, too, who went the other way. (Hear, hear.) Councillor LORD: These advocates of smoke and the orchid-growers always manage to live on that side of the town where there is no smoke. (Laughter.) I CouncillorEvaNs said their inspectors carried out their ! duties without seeking to hamper manufacturers. (Hear, : hear.) It was a serious matter to put unnecessary diffi- ' culties in their way. When smoke was emitted owing to thoughtlessness and recklessness, the inspectors spoke Total 3-8 to those in authr,rity, and they did their best to have the nuisance abated. They did not think they ought as MACKIE'S V. WALTON ST. MARY'S (LIVERPOOL).— a committee to take extreme steps. Efforts had heen Played at Walton on Saturday. Scores :—Mackie's, made and were still being made to improve the con- (for7Bl seven wickets) ; Walton St. Mary's, 39. ditions of infant ife. (Hear, hear.) i The minutes were carried.
