MAILSIILIOUSE-LANE.—Played on I Alderman Ev tNs moved the adoption of the Gas the ground of the former on Saturday. Scores : Committee's minutes. The committee reported that Trinity, 42; Marsahouse-lane, 23. the annual balance sheet of the gas undertaking sub- mitted by the ..Secretary showed a balance of £23,251
WALKER'S BREWERY V. WILDERSPOOL BREWRRY.— Played on the •ground of the former on Saturday. bcores :—Walker's Brewery, 36; Wilderspool Brewery, 35.

16s. Gd., out of which, after providing for the renewals necessary in the works, the sum of £ll,OOO would be available for the reduction of the rates. The resolu- tion, said Alderman Evans, had been placed on the agenda as the committee were anxious to change the I system of dealing with their profits. Alderman Evans I gave a history of the gas undertaking since it was acquired by the Corporation in order to show firstly. ; the truublous times through which it had passed, and secondly, to instance the steady increase in the profits ' during the past few years, which profits had without doubt very materially assisted the rates. At the present time, he said, we are faced with the fact that in the very near future several renewals and replacements, which have been referred to, will have to be made. To meet these the committee have no avilable fund, the reserve fund not being applicable as according to our powers this fund must not be used except for the purpose of meeting some unexpected calamity. It, therefore, behoves the committee as , business men to make some provision to meet this ex- ' penditure, so that the whole of the burden will not fall upon one year. The committee advise that a sufficient sum should from time to time be carried forward on I the floating or working balance, so that when the time I does come, it will find them prepared to meet the very I heavy charge without disorganizing the profits for that I particular year, and more especially without affecting the rates, which to a great extent are dependent upon the profit transferred from the gas undertaking. The working balsnce at present is not sufficient to be drawn upon for any extraordinary expenditure, being only large enough for the comfortable working of the con- cern; indeed the banking account has been overdrawn for a period during last year. It has been the custom for the last few years, when preparing the estimates for the requirements of the town, to put down a sum as likely to be earned by the gas undertaking. In every case this sum has been exceeded. When preparing for the year 1905-6 £lO,OOO was the amount named, £14,181 19s. Bid. was realized. I do not think it will be disputed, that the transferring of this large sum had considerable influence in deciding the Finance Committee in recom- mending the reduction of 4d. in the £ on the rates. The amount agreed to for the year 1906-7 was £ll,OOO ; the net amount of profit is found to be £14,700 17s. 11d.—a record. We have this year a favourable opportunity of commencing such a scheme. I say favourable advisedly, as we are, Ibelieve, on the.eee of very strenuous times owing to the increased price of coals and the decrease of revenue, owing to the recent reduced price of gas. The contracts for coals have just been settled for the year at 2s. W. per ton advance, which means an extra cost of £5,000. and the reduction in the price of gas means a decrease in the revenue of £3,000. Consequently there will be a charge against the year's profits of .£B,OOO. Against this we have only as a set-off the normal increase in the consumption of gas. and what may be an abnormal increase owing to the reduction in price. You will, therefore, agree that all facts point to this being our opportunity, which if allowed to go by we may find it will be a considerable time before we are again in this happy position of having profits in excess of the estimate. It is therefore, proposed by the com- mittee that £ [l,OOO be transferred in reduction of the rates, leaving the balance to be carried forward. In dealing with the profits in this manner, we are following the excellent example of other COrpora- tions. Our neighbours, St. Helens, last year made a profit of 28,218, out of which sum :.5.000 was allocated to the relief of the rates. We are taking, to my mind, the very wise policy of not parting with all our profits, but retaining a sum out of prosperous years, which has the effect of more equitably disposing of the profits and increasing our working balance to such an amount as will save us from possible disaster. Councillor DUNCAN seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor CLEGG congratulated the committee, managers and rank and file of the Gas Department upon their past year's work. They had made a profit of .E 23,351 or an increase upon the previous year of £506. That profit had been made after the reduction of 2d. in the price of gas since last November. He did not think it was the duty of the Committee to ear mark what profit should be used for. Since the reduction in November the ratepayers bad had a further reduction of 4d. in the rates, but no reduction had been made in slot meter rents. He understood there were 8,000 slot meters in Warrington and those who rented them received no advantage Warrington, the reduction in the price of gas. It was time they were considered. To alter the meters would cost roughly £l,OOO, and he suggested that sum should be set aside fer the purpese. Alderman EVANS said the Committee had no power to create a separate fund. The DEPUTY MAYOR said it was not the time to con- sider slot meters or anything else until they knew what profit would be available after allowing for the increased cost of coal. They had to have a reserve in case of an explosion at the gas works or some other contingency.

Councillor PEMBERTON said he did not see why one class of consumer should be considered any more than another. There was no reason why discount should not be allowed. The capital account of the gas department was a very important question, and it would be better to be considered at a special meeting of the General Pur- poses Committee. If the resolution meant they were going to set up a new principle he did not think it was fair. It was not right that the present generation should provide for future renewals out of profit,the cost of which should be spread over 30 or 50 years. If they wanted to renew the plant they should borrow the money. The ratepayers ought to enjoy the profits. He did not believe in the present generation paying more than they ought to pay. He was sorry the question had been sprung on them. They ought to have the state- ment of Alderman Evans printed and circulated to every Councillor. He could not grasp it in its entirety. If it was going to alter the system altogether they ought to have had notice of it, and he thought it would be well to withdraw the resolution so that they could consider the matter in the meantime. _ _

Councillor STEEL said there was no resolution on that question before them. The MAYOR said that was so. There was only a state- ment by Alderman Evans. Councillor NIELD was also in favour of the statement being printed. Alderman TINNION said the committee had given the matter careful consideration, and as business men he thought what they had in their minds and what they intended to recommend to the Council was the proper thing to do. During the last few years they had handed over very large sums for the reduction of the rates. The sums previous to 1904 were comparatively small. After having put the works on an up-to-date footing in 1903-4 they had a considerable sum available for the reduction of the rates. The 4d. taken off the rates last year, he thought,was a mistake,and it would not have been taken off had it not been for the extraordinary profit shown by the gas undertaking, the whole of the reduction coming out of excessive profits for that year. The committee did not wish to repeat the mistake of handing over more than their profits to relieve the rates. The gas holders might bold out for a few months or they might hold out for a few years, but the time had arrived when they must make provision for the entire replating or renewal of a gas holder, which would cost four or five thousand pounds. They could have taken that amount out of one year if they had high profits, but the days of high profits were over. They had now to pay four or five thousand more for coal, and they had decreased the selling price of gas to the extent of about £3,000, so that there was £B,OOO to come out of the gas undertaking next year. At the same time they had to face four or five thousand pounds more expenditure—a total difference, probably, of £12,000 in the sum available for profits. It affected not only the gas consumer but the ratepayer, because the rates had for some time been dependent on a large sum being contributed. They wanted to keep the rates as low as possible, but above all to keep them uniform. The committee had consulted the Borough Treasurer, ' who represented the Finance Committee, and he had made provision for this year for the sum of £ll,OOO. Why should the committee hand over all the money when they saw in the near future all this expenditure staring them in the face? Were the Council prepared to negative the idea the Gas Committee had in sug- gesting that £ll,OOO should be handed over, and have as a result the rates varying up and down, or were they going to leave the matter in the hands of men who thoroughly understood it? Councillor BALL thought the Committee were justi- fied in making the fullest possible provision for renewals. There was, however, no resolution approving the course snggested by the Gas Committee. Councillor TINNION said Jae would not hesitate to move a resolution at the next committee meeting to confirm their suggestions, but they thought they ought to take the Council into their confidence first, so that the members would have the opportunity of thinking the matter over.

Councillor WILKINSON deplored the fact that the Council reduced the rates last year by 4d., because they could have done very well with the money in reserve. They wished to put aside .£3,700, to increase the floating capital. in order to do the alterations necessary. If the alterations were to be paid for out of one year's profits, it would mean 7d. on the rates.

Alderman EVANS said the question of a reduction to slot meter users had been under consideration for twelve months. The Committee were unanimous that something should be done, 134 they could not agree as to the course to be adopted. However, they were pledged to something.

Th`e minutes were aptroved. , THE TRAMWAYS. A PLEA FOR THE MANCHESTER-ROAD EXTESION. OTHER DISTRICTS TO BE CONSIDERED. At a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee the advisability of obtaining extended time for the construction of tramways to Bruche Bridge and Padgade Bridge was considered and the tramways manager having reported that in his opinion the ex- tension of those tramways would involve a considerable financial loss it was resolved that no application be made for an extension of time. The balance sheet of the tramways undertaking for the year ended 31st March last, showing a net profit of £1,309 17s. 10d. on the year's working, was received. It was resolved,that the salary of the tramways manager be increased by the sum of £25 per annum. The MAYOR in moving the adoption of the minutes sail the gross profits on the tramways undertaking amounted to £7,093 9s. Gd. 88 against £6,285 6s. sd. for the corresponding period last year. div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
THE DISPOSAL OF THE GAS PROFITS.
Tramway Extensions Wanted

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Town Hall on Tueiday. The Mayor presided and there were present :—The Deputy Mayor (Alderman Bolton) ; Aldermen A. Bennett, John Evans, W. J. Forshaw, R. W. Francomb, D. Tinnion ,• Councillors T. H. Ashcroft, J. Ball, T. Barton, W. Benson, T. Chantler, W. Clegg, E. Cunning. ton, J. Dickenson, D. S. Duncan, James Evans, L. Ellison, J. Hawthoin, Dr. Joseph, J. Lord, J. J. Nield, J. Pemberton, J. Sankey, J. Skelland, T. S. Steel, J, Fulton-Smith, 0. Toole, G. T. Wilding, J. Wilkinson, W. J. Wilson; Messrs. J. L. Whittle (Town Clerk), A. T. Hallaway (Deputy Town Clerk),T. Longdin (Borough Surveyor), J. Peas (Water Engineer), W. S. Haddock (Gas Engineer), F. V. L. Mathias, (Electrical Engineer). J. M. Murray (Director of Education), F. G. Rud- dock (Borough Analyst. Tilt GROWTH OF TOWNS. THE REGCLATION OF NEW AREAS.

The MAYOR moved :—" That this Council do approve lof the scheme for a Town Planning Bill adopted by the Council of the Association of iVluncipal Corporations on the 13th June. 1907, and respectfully requests the Government to introduce legislation to this effect." The motion, said the Mayor, was., the outcome of a meeting of the Association of Municipal Corporations held in London in June. The scheme referred to pro- vided for giving powers to local authorities to prescribe and regulate the planning of their areas in regard to the laving out of streets in connection with building schemes, empowering local authorities to appoint com- mittees to deal with the subject and to co-opt persons who were not members on such committees. The object of the motion was to bring about a better state of affairs by preventing overcrowding in new districts,and putting an end to the haphazard,piecemeal development of urban districts, which, to use the words of a report prepared on the subject by a special committee which trid considered the matter,"was disastrous to the public health and ruinous to the public purse." Alderman BENNETT seconded, and said this was one of the most important proposals that had ever been brought before the notice of the Council. Its ultimate issue affected the whole future of all the towns in the country. He was glad to think that in Warrington they had made substantial ptogress during the last few years towards making a beautiful and attractive town. They had had help from various voluntary associations, and it was pleasant to him to feel that in this good work, which ought to devolve on municipalities, they had had the assistance of the Beautiful Warrington Society and other societies who were trying to keep the Council up to their duty. He did not know why it should be necessary for private enterprise to provide wholesome and sanitary dwellings in the suburbs; it should be one of the first duties of a community to map out its future and the town should have control over its fate. At the present time they had no such control. They wanted to have the power to retain land they bought and not to have to sell what remained after they had made improvements and they ought also to have the power to build or regulate buildings. He was delighted they were to have a spacious circus at Market-gate, but he had his doubts as to whether it might not be spoilt,as they bad not sufficient control over buildings to be erected there. He reminded the Council that in 1895 he proposed the following resolution, which was adopted : That it be an instruction to the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee in framing new bylaws, as recom- mended by the Local Government Board, to consider whether the existing regulations as to the width of new streets and passagef are inadequate,, having regard 0, the probable growth of the town, and whether it would not be possible for the committee to reserve the right to exercise some effective supervision over the general arrangement of the new building sites, so as to ensure that all new thoroughfares shall be convenient and symmetrical, and that open spaces shall be provided in every area." He was sorry to say nothing had been! done, and the resolution bad proved a dead letter. It bad cost a quarter of a million to widen Bridge-street yet they were allowing, with their eyes open, streets to be made which would be entirely inadequate for the future, and their children's children would have to undo their schemes in order to repair the errors they had in their shortsightedness committed. He hoped that in the future it would be made impossible for anyone to perpetrate the monstrosities'which had been perpetrated in their industrial towns in the past. The resolution was approved. •Cheshire Licences to go. HIS CRITICS. div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON
NEW CHIEF CONSTABLE.
The Examiner, Saturday July 6, 1907.

sions. You qtote from a descriptive letter by Mr. Wilson., M.P., in the " Daily News" where, after some very encouraging remarks, he suggests a little mare force. May I just say in passing that I thought on this first occasion my friends in the Constituency would prefer that one did not make the speech a Party fillipic. Again thanking them all for their kindness, I have the honour to remain, your obedient servant,
A. H. CROSFIELD,
Hyde Park Hotel, London, July 3rd, 1907.

Sir,—Mr. Crosfield's critics are various if not numerous, and their letters which have recently appeared show how utterly impossible it is for a Member of Parliament to please all persons. I think some of Mr. Crosfield's critics forget that he was returned at the last election to represent this con- stituency in Parliament and, although we are very pleased to see him when opportunity offers, yet I think everyone knows that

MS FIRST DUTY is the House of Commons, and with the exception of the period of his breakdown in health after the severe strain of the General Election his attendances in Parliament, I think, must have been gratifying to all his friends, if not to his opponents. But Mr. Crosfield does not neglect Warrington. He was here with as when General Buller visited the town. He was present and entertained the 'Liberal agents of Cheshire and Lancashire when they held their conference here. He also came to Warrington on the occasion of the excursion of the footballers to Chester, when he so magnificently entertained them, and recently he addressed a splendid meeting in the Parr Hall at which he gave us his promise that he would annually render an account of his political stewardship. His speech in the House, by what I can hear in the town, seems to have given general satisfaction, and after our past experience with Tory members I think we may safely say that for attention to political duties and local requirements, we have at the present time the best Member Warrington ever did itself the credit to return to Parliament. Our late Member was an
AD3IIRABLE REPRESENTATIVE FOR • THE ISLAND OF CYPRUS

but our present Member pays much more attention to Warrington and its requirements. It is rather laughable that our Tory friends should complain of Mr. Crosfield's want of attention to his Parliamentary and local duties after the singular experience we have passed through during the recent period of Tory rule. It is many years since Warrington had a member so devoted to its interests both here and in St. Stephen's, and although we all know that it is totally impossible for any man to please both friend and foe, yet I think those of us who voted for Mr. Crosfield at the last election will be perfectly satisfied with his performances up to the present moment and I have no doubt that as time passes we shall have still greater cause to congratulate ourselves upon the

contracts of the Abram Coal Co., Ltd., and Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Ltd.. for the supply of gas coal; tthe contract of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Ltd for the supply of slack to the water works; and the agreement with the Lancashire County Council for the maintenance and repair of main roads during the year ending the 31st March, 1908.

div.head: REMARKABLE DEMONSTaMON OF COMMONSENSE
div.p: REMARKABLE DEMONSTaMON OF COMMONSENSE

which the voters of this borough exhibited at the last election. Many matters of immense importance will be submitted to the House of Commons before long and we can rely upon our Radical Member to give a loyal and enthusiastic support to the party of reform, backed up and assisted as he generally is by the Labour members in the House, to bring about a better day for those who have to win their bread by the industry of their hands.—Yours &c., July 4th, 1907.

div.head: :NEW ORGAN AT BOLD-STREET
div.p: :NEW ORGAN AT BOLD-STREET
CHURCH.
A Fine Instrument.

Thursday next will be a red letter day in the history of Bold-street Wesleyan Church for it will witness the dedication and opening of the new organ. A special service will be held at 7.30 the featare of which will be an organ recital by Dr. J. Kendrick Pyne, organist of the Cathedral, University, and to the Corporation of Manchester, who will sub- mit a classical programme including " Grand Prelude and Fugue in E Minor" (Bach.) Mrs. Arthur Booth will give vocal solos. On the following Sunday the special services will be continued an .1 sermons will be preached by the Rev. Samuel T. House, of .Liverpool. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. 83C., Viet., Will preside at the organ and at the close of the evening service will give a recital. On Thursday, the 18th inst, there will be recitals at 3.30 and 7.30 by Mr. David Clegg (of Crystal Palace and Queen's Hall, London), who will interpret attractive programmes of music in various styles. On Sunday the 21st inst the Rev. Joseph Manning will preach and at the close of the evening service Mr. Frank Hickman will give a recital and choruses will be rendered by the War- rington Male Voice Prize choir under the conductorshin of Mr. S. Hassall. Admission to the Thursday recitals is by souvenir copies of which can be obtained from the committee at a charge of is. and 6d. respectively. The opening of this magnificent instrument which has been built by Messrs. Brindley and Foster, Sheffield, London and Glasgow, marks the consummation of a scheme which was inaugurated in 1901. The Rev. Joseph Manning, in an introductory letter in the souvenir, points out that in that year under the leader ship of the Rev. Theodore Bishop a fund wa started and about £2OO was raised by subscriptions, con certs and various other efforts. Nothing further was done in the matter until 1906 when the trustees initiated a scheme for the liquidation of the church debts, the renovation of the church, and the erection of a new organ.On receiving the report of an expert who was con- bulted,the trustees decided to purchase a new organ and Dr. Andrew Carnegie,on being appealed to, very kindly offered to give £430 towards the cost of the instrument. This splendid offer was gratefully accepted and a com- mittee was appointed to proceed with the necessary steps for building the organ. Six first-class firms were invited to tender. Aft& receiving expert advice on the specifications and tenders, the competitors were reduced to two. The Committee visited Bolton, Liver- pool, and Barrow-in-Furness and examined organs built by these two firms, the result being that Messrs. Brindley and Foster were entrusted with the order. The cost of the organ is £9OO. The committee (Rev. J. Manning, Messrs. F. Pendle- bury, F. Hickman and G. E. Guest) state that their aim throughout the whole of the negotiations has been to , ensure that there should be installed in the Church a really musical organ, and one possessed of every modem feature of manipulative mechanism,l and it is unquestionable that their labours in this direction have been crowned with success. It is not only possible to employ swell, great, and choir organs for ordinary service uses, but the player is enabled to easily obtain a series of solo effects which are not possible of attainment on any ordinary two manual organ. The action of the instrument is the latest form of tubular pneumatic, and it is blown by Brindley and Foster's motor, the cost of current working out at one penny per hour.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDING. – Richardson —Hazlehurst.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDING. - Richardson —Hazlehurst.

There was a large congregation at the Church of Our Lady (St. Mary's), Latchford, to witness the marriage of Miss May Hazleharst, daughter of Mr. Thomas Hazehurst, Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath, and Mr. James Ashton Richardson, son of Mr. John Richardson, Allen-street. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. H. E. Hazle- burst, D.D., brother of the bride, Newport, Salop, assisted by the Rev. Father Marrs, Latchford. The bride, who was given away by her father was charmingly attired in a dress of white silk, trimmed with Valenciennes la ce,and also wore a veil surmounted by a wreath of orange blossom. Her bouquet was of lilies and carnations and she wore a pearl necklace and gold cross the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Miss Bibby and Miss Roddy, and their dresses were of fawn voile and hats of Wedgewood blue. They carried bouquets of white flowers and wore gold brooches, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. J. Richardson, brother of the bridegroom, was at the organ and contributed a number of appropriate selections. The reception was held at the Hall Cafe, Stockton Heath, after which the happy couple left for Scarborough for the honeymoon, the bride travelling in a dress of wine coloured Venetian cloth, and a Tuscan hat to match. Many beautiful presents were received.

div.head: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
Retirement of Mr. Rathbone.

After over forty years' service Mr. Rathbone has retired from the managership of the Warrington Co-operative Society, his resignation to take effect on the 13th inst. Mr. Rathbone has held the dual position of marager and secretary and during the long period in which he has been at the bead of the Society the annual turnover has grown from £2545 to £150,000, largely owing to his devoted and faithful service. This, it will be remembered, was fittingly recognized in 1995 when the members presented him with 300 guineas and a framed photograph. It has been decided in the future to separate the two offices held by Mr. Rathboge and applications for both are invited.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
CYCLIST DASHED AGAINST A HOUSE.

Arthur Ignatius Green, aged eighteen, apprentice glasscutter, 54, Shaw-street, died in the Providence Hospital, St. Helens, on Saturthy evening. He lived with his brother. On Sunday afternoon, the 23rd ult., he went cycling. At the top of Liverpool-road he was was seen to approach at a terrific speed, and dash across the road right against the front of the " Red, White, and Blue " beerhouse. The bicycle was smashed to pieces, and Green thrown violently against the wall. He stated that when he was coming down Borough- road he lost control of the machine. He quickly lapsed , into unconsciousness, and never recovered.

div.head: -"AFRAID OF HIS LIM."
div.p: -"AFRAID OF HIS LIM."

William Anders, of Fleet-lane, was charged at St Helens with threatening to kill James M'Henry, watch- man at the Ashton's Green Colliery; and James Anders, the son, was charged with committing an assault on M.'Henry. Prosecutor made out 4, very strong case of threats, and said that the elder man swore most emphatically that he would knifA him. Later the younger Anders struck him in the thToat. He was afraid of his life, and dare not bring any witnesses.— Anders denied the offences, and said that M.'Henry had violently assaulted one of his boys.—Defendants were ordered to find sureties or go to gaol for fourteen clays.

div.head: CHILDREN TRAINED TO STEAL.
div.p: CHILDREN TRAINED TO STEAL.

Mrs. Emma Wilkinson, of Sutton-road, was charged at St. Helens, on Monday, along with her two little girls, with stealing and receiving 2s. 6d. worth of lead piping from houses in course of erection in Helena- road, Sutton. The evidence was that a quantity of lead was missed, and the watchman sarr the girls go and tear the lead off the buildings. Police Constable Harvey arrested the girls, and found that Mrs. Wilkinson had sold the lead.--The Chief Constable said Mrs. Wilkinson had been eight times convicted, seven of them for stealing. He was sorry to say she was training the children to be thieves. On two occasions this year he cautioned her about sending the children out to steal. She was educating them to go and watch for children going on errands, when they spoke to them and asked to see how much money they had. If the children were confiding enough to show the money it was promptly snatched out of their hands.—lnspector Dunn said in one case 2s. was taken, and in another sixpence.— Sergeant Stewart said Owe girls took two ounces of tobacco out of another girl s basket only last week.— The Chairman (Alderman Martin) said the woman had a long list. It was the most shocking thing possible for her to be sending the children out to steal. They must be taken away from her. Hannah, aged twelve, must go to a reformatory for five years, and Elizabeth, aged ten, must b(io to an Industrial school until she was fourteen. Mrs. Wilkinson must go to gaol for three months, a similar sentence to which she served last year.

div.head: VOLUNTEER CHURCH PARADES. LONG SERVICE MEDALS PRESENTED AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: VOLUNTEER CHURCH PARADES. LONG SERVICE MEDALS PRESENTED AT ST. HELENS.

The 2nd Lancashire Royal Engineers (Volunteers) on Sunday held their annual church parade, when 250 officers and men attended afternoon service at St. Thomas's Church. Sixty members of the Widnes section attended, under the leadership of Regimental Colonel J. P. Fraser. The other officers were :—Captains Bertram Brewis, J. Haslam Fox, C. T. Brown, H. L. Campbell, and C. Anders, Lieutenants G. Oppenheim, W. F. Dixon-Nuttall, and G. Lomax, Adjutant A. C. Dobson, Acting-Chaplain Rev. L. J. Rich, and Sergeant-Major E. J. Hannaford. The service wa9 con- ducted by the Rev. L. J. Rich, who preached an inter- esting address on "Character." He said that a man could only be valued by the character he bore. Every- one made his own character, which grew as he grew; good or bad, it was his own making. When a man died he took nothing from this world but his character, and then be must face eternity with the character he had made. Later, on returning to the drill hall, Colonel Fraser presented a long service and good conduct medal to Sergeant-instructor R. Peachey, and Volunteer long service medals to Sappers H. Naylor (A Company) and F. R. Sherwood (Field Company).—The annual church parade of the St. Helens (B) Squadron of the Lancashire Hussars Imperial Yeomanry was held on Sunday afternoon at St.Helens Parish Church. Over ninety officers and men paraded in front of the Town Hall, under the command of Captain A. L. Pilkington. There were also present Lieutenant Bromilow, Captain W. G. Dixon, Regimental Sergeant-Major A. Heaton, Sergeant-Major W. Cook, Squadron Sergeant-Major Holt, and Sergeant-Major Lambert. The regimental band, under Bandmaster T. Batley, headed the march to the church, and accompanied the various hymns. There was a large congregation, including the members of the men's Bible class. The Rev. C. F. Trench conducted the service, and the Rev. H. S. Broadbent, curate-in- charge, preached on" Citizenship," and eulogised the services of the various sections of the Volunteer Army.

div.head: WIRRAL AGRICULURAL SHOW.
div.p: THE WIRRAL AGRICULURAL SHOW.

The total entries for the Wirral and Birkenhead Show to be held next Wednesday and Thursday number 5000 and include many champion exhibits from the Great International Horse Show at Olympia, and also many of the winning exhibits at the show of the Royal Society of England, held last week. The cattle and dairy exhibits surpass those of previous years. The four-in- hand class consists of five entries and will form a most attractive exhibit, while the Coach Horn Blowing Competition, entries for which will be accepted up to noon on the first day of the Show—will be certain to create further interest to intending visitors. The entries in the Dog Section are particularly strong. while the Poultry, Pigeon, Rabbit and Cavy Sections are also equally well represented-, so that given fine weather the society should have a very successful Show.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT TO NORTH WALES.
div.p: ROYAL VISIT TO NORTH WALES.

In connection with the visit to North Wales of their , Majesties the King and Queen, special sea excursions have been arranged by the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Co., Limited, by their steamer St. Tudno, ' from the Prince's Landing-stage. The Holyhead excur- , sions, which are advertised for Mondays and Wednes- days, will no doubt be taken advantage of on Monday, July Bth, by those who tire desirous of seeing the King's Yacht in Holyhead Harbour and the squadron of war- ships which will be in attendance as escort in connection with the Royal visit. On Tuesday, 9th inst, the St. Tudno will leave Liverpool for Llandudno and Bsgnor, allowing four hours ashore at the Athens of Wales, and giving ample time to all who may be desirous of wit- nessing the ceremony of the laying of the foundation stone of the University College new buildings by his Majesty. After the ceremony the Royal Party will take a motor journey through the various places of interest, and her Majesty the Queen will during the afternoon drive through Menai Bridge to Beaumaris on a visit to Sir Richard Williams-Bulkeley, Bart. Passengers by the North Wales steamer La Marguerite at 10.45 a.m. will have ample time ashore at Beautuaris to see her Majesty drive through the town.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
DEATH OF "DR." GERRARD, WIDNES.

By the demise of Mr. Thomas Gerrard, aged fifty- even, familiarly known throughout South-West Lanca- hire as "the Doctor," Widnes loses one of its best-known • figures. He resided in Widnes all his life. Two years ago he fell a victim to paralysis, which con- fined him to his room. He lived unconscious of his surroundings for months. Thirty-eight years a licensee, he latterly held the licence of the Alexandra Hotel. He was chairman of the Widnes and St. Helens Licensed Victuallers' Association, and was their delegate many times at conferences. His benevolence during the colliers' strike and his connection with the soup kitchen will long be remembered by the poor of the town. It was he who originated and gave the newsboys' treat. He sat in the Town Council for three years. DEATH OF MR. F. H. GOSSAGE.

We regret to announce the death of Mr. Frederick Herbert Gossage, J.P., which took place at eight o'clock on Sunday night at his residence, Camp Hill, Wool ton, in his seventy-fifth year.—By the death of Mr. Gossage, who was head of the widely-known firm of William Gossage and Sons, soapmakers, a serious public loss has been sustained by both Liverpool and Widnes. The bnsiness, now of world-wipe reputa- tion, was established by Mr. William Gossage, a manufacturing chemist of distinguished ability, who utilised the value of silicate of soda in reducing the cost and improving the manufacture of soap. Mr. F. H. Gossage was the third son of Mr. W. Gossage. He joined his father in the conduct of the business, which was carried on at Widnes. Under his father's supervision he was initiated into the principles and mysteries of practical chemistry, and himself became a distinguished chemist. To begin with, however, the business of the firm was confined to the smelting of copper; but in 1855 Mr. William Gossage worked out his useful discovery,and the manufacture of soap was entered upon with a success which is now a matter of public record The development of the great works of the firm at Widnes, affording employment for a multitude of work- men, has contributed very largely to the growth of the town. In Widnes and its welfare Mr. Gossage always took a keen interest. He was for many years a member of the old Local Board, and for a considerable period its chairman. When Widnes was, in no slight degree owing to his efforts, incorporated in 1892, he was offered and •Iccepted the position of first Mayor.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON

MINER'S SUDDEN DEATH. An Earlestown man named Worthington, who was employed at the Old Boston Colliery, Haydock, was taken suddenly ill after going down the pit on Monday and died. WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH PICNIC. Tha Welsh Congregational Church Sunday School held their annual picnic on Saturday. The party num- bering about 30, left Earlestown at 8.45 arriving in Southport at 10.30. The principal places of interest were visited, and driving and boating were indulged in. The party assembled at Mr. Baker's cafe for dinner and tea: An enjoyable day was spent, and, leaving South- port at 8.30, the party arrived in Earlestown shortly after ten. The arrangements were well carried out by Messrs. Pearce and Jones. ALLEGED THEFT OF A MARE AND TRAP. At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, before Mr. Charles White, Garrett Ronayne, High-st., Newton-le-Willows, was again brought up, ciarged with stealing a bay mare, a trap, and a set of harness value £5O, the property or his father,Williarns Ronayne. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the defendant.— William Ronayne said his sons had done this tort of thing many times. He did not think his son had any intention of stealing.—Edward Rogers, licenses of the Legh Arms, Golborne, said defendant wanted to sell the horse and trap to him for £3o.—The case was dismissed. WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOLS. An interesting presentation was made last Friday night in the Lecture Hall of the Wesleyan Chumh. Mr. 'John Roberts, on behalf of the managers and teachers, !past and present,of the Wesleyan Day Schools presented Mr. Gooding with a roll-top desk and Mrs. Gooding with an invalid bed-table and writing desk combined. The gifts were a slight acknowledgment of the valuable services of Mr. Gooding as secretary and correspondent of the above schools for the past 25 years. Mr. C. Burgess, headmaster, Mrs. Grundy (headmistress of the Infants' School), Mr. E. T. Evans, and several others addressed the meeting, all speaking of the valuable services rendered by Mr. Gooding to the school. Mr. and Mrs. Gooding, who were deeply moved,thanked the donors very cordially. MR. SEDDON, M.P., AT LANCASTER. "A SHAH BATTLE" WITH THE LORDS. Mr. Seddon, M.P., addressing a Labour meeting at Lancaster on gaturday night, said he had no faith in othe sham battle against the House of Lords, because during the past few days the Prime Minister had made four more members of that House. No party had made more peers that the Liberal party during the past 60 years. With what result? They had a mere remnant in the Lipp€F.House, which demonstrated that whatever a man was in the House of Commons in the House of Lords he sided with privilege and monopoly. Mr. Seddon had no faith in the motion passed by the Govern- ment or its intentions with regard to the Lords. —Mr. Seddon referred to his experience at the Royal garden party at Windsor. He said he thought he would go and see the gentlemen who flattered the Labour party in the smokeroom of the House of Commons in their own haunts, basking in the sunshine of Royalty. As a result he was confirmed in his conviction that the aristocracy had learned nothing and forgotten nothing, that they were just as brutal and would exercise the same power, if they had it, that they did in the French Revolution. He saw on the faces of high-born dames at this garden party an utter contempt for the classes to which the workers belonged. He saw women there who sneered at the wife of the working man—at the wives of man who on 30s. a week had done more for the Empire than high-born ladies with £30,000 a year.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
CORPORATION'S PROPOSAL TO SUPPLY ELECTRICITY. Threatened Opposition. SPITTLE BRIDGE IMPROVEMENT.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednes- day when there were present :—Dr. Murray (presiding) Messrs. G. Mather, W. Furness,A. Brookes,J. Backhouse W. Stanier, J. Ball, W. Houghton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor ), H. H. Burnage (assistant surueyor), F. W. lierfoot -(inspector), and Dr. Sephton (medical officer). CORPORATION AND ELECTRIC POWER SUPPLY.

The CLERK reported the receipt of a communication from the Town Clerk of Warrington informing him that in December next the Corporation intended to apply for a provisional order for the supply of electricity in the area of the District Council.

Mr. BROOKS : If it means they want a monopoly I will go most strongly against it. We have had enough of their water monopoly. Mr. SUTTON: The point is can you supply electricity ? Mr. BROOKE : No, but we can perhaps place the parishes in a better position that they would he in if Warrington got the monopoly. If it were not for Warrington having the water monopoly we could have got a supply for Glazebrook at a considerably less cost.
Mr. MATHER : And for other places as well.

Mr. BROOKES : I certainly object to Warrington or anyone else getting a monopoly which we cannot break through in years to come. It would be a short-sighted policy to allow it. The CLERK: I will ask the Town Clerk for a copy of the proposed Order. Mr. MATHER : lam prepared to move that we oppose the granting of the Order. It was decided that the Clerk should obtain a copy of the Order.

div.head: WINWICK ROAD LIGHTING.
div.p: WINWICK ROAD LIGHTING.
The CLERK reported that the Committee of visitors to to the Winwick Asylum had written urging the Council to take steps in regard to the Lighting of the Winwick-road.
Mr. NEWCOMBE explained that the matter was being considered by a special Committee appointed toodecide upon the number of lamps to be erected. IMPROVENTENT AT SA'NKEY.

At the last meeting of the Council the Surveyor was deputed to wait upon Mr. Knowles, Sankey, to induce him to give up a small plot of land for the purpose of road improvement at Sankey. Mr. Newcombe reported that Mr. Knowles had agreed to give the land. r. Knowles was rather disappointed that it had been published in the Press that the plot of land for which he originally asked £3 was only three yards square as from time to time he had given other plots for purposes of public improvements.________

div.head: MAINTENANCE OF MAIN ROADS.
div.p: THE MAINTENANCE OF MAIN ROADS.

The CLERK stated that the Settle District Council had resolved "That in the opinion of this Council the time has now arrived when main roads should be made a national charge," and asked the Warrington Council to pass a similar resolution and forward it to the Local Government Board. Mr. BnocutEs said he would like the Council to sub- scribe to the principle and moved that a similar resolu- tion be approved. Mr. BACKUOUSE seconded and the motion was approved.

div.head: DANGEROUS SPOTS AT BURTONWOOD.
div.p: DANGEROUS SPOTS AT BURTONWOOD.

The Buttonwood Parish Council forwarded a letter pointing out that there were several very sharp turns in the roads in the parish, and, as .the roads were fre- quently filled with children' asking that the District Council should erect signals in the village warning drivers of vehicles to observe caution. Mr. NEWCOMB said the Parish Council had also written to him asking that the Council should erect iron fences opposite to the entrances to the schools, and on ,the edge of the footpith. This was to prevent children rushing out of the school grounds on to the roadway. The question of the erection of the danger signals was one for the County Council. Mr. MATHER said that with regard to the fence he thought it would be better if the barrier were erected in the school grounds. Mr. NEWCOMBE: If the proposed fence were erected it would be an obstruction and anyone would be entitled to break it down. THE INSPECTION OF ALKALI WORKS.

The question of a contribution by the Council towards the salary of an inspector of alkali works in the Widnes and Rnncorn area came up for consideration. Mr. NEWCOMBE said he had waited upon the solici- tors whom he found were acting for a Committee of Landowners. They suggested that a resident inspector should be appointed by the Local Government Board, half his salary to be paid by that Board and half by a number of authorities. They also suggested the appoint- ment of another inspector, whose salary would be paid by the Committ,e of Landowners. Mr. BACKHOUSE explained that Cuerdley and Penketh were the only districts in the area of the Council affected by the Widnes and Runcorn works. The last inspector retired in December, and he could speak from personal kdowledge that the gases emitted were very much worse now than previously. rhose gases were dangerous to the community, and he would be sorry if the inspectorship were done away with. Mr. MATHER : I agree that a resident inspector should be appointed but the last one lived at Southport. Mr. BACKHOUSE : But he came daily to Widnes.
It was decided to agree to contrilinte to the half salary of an inspector in proportion to the area affected—Cuerdley, Penketh and Sankey. SPITTLE BRIDGE.

Mr. MATHER moved "That the County Main Roads and Bridges Committee having definity declined to sanction adoption of the larger scheme in connection , with the Spittle Bridge improvement, this Council take the necessary steps for the work being carried out according to the smaller scheme as shown on the plan submitted by the County Bridgemaster on November 20th, 1906." The Surveyor' he said, had supplied a list of the prices asked for the land required for the improvement. He would like to ask if those prices were final? They appeared to him to be very ex- horbitant and personally he would not give them by any means. Mr.NßwcomßE : I have seen the landowners and they will not take less. Mr. HOUGHTON: lam not satisfied. Are there no compulsory powers? Mr. MATHER : If we go to arbitration it will mean a big expense. Mr. BROOKLS asked if the bridge could be temporarily repaired. Probably before the present Government was out of office, at any rate before many years were over, they would have greater powers with regard to pur- chases of that kind, and he thought they might delay the improvement until they had those powers. Mr. HOUGHTON: If you start repairing the whole thing witl come about our ears. Mr..IVIATRER said he was prepared to move that the Surveyor offer 6d. per square yard for the land. He thought that was ample, in fact more than the land was worth.

Mr. FURNESS : It seems to me that two or three plots are worth more. I don't think Mr. Mather is quite in order in suggesting that the whole should be paid for at a uniform rate. Mr. BALL: Mr. Mather's offer is £l4O per acre and £5O would boa big price. Mr. NEWCOMBE said the bridge could be repaired but it would not be a cheap job. It would cost about £55. Mr. FURNESS moved that the Surveyor prepare an estimate of the cost of repairing the bridge. Mr. HOUGHTON : The bridge is totally inadequate and it is breaking down. I would not be surprised and I would be very pleased when I get home to find that it has broken down. I don't care at all for the idea of tinkering with an old bridge. Mr. SUTTON: You are in this position. The land- owners think you have only Hobson's choice and it is for you to show them that is not the case.
Mfr. FURNESS' su4gestioa was approved. THE HEATH OF THE DISTRICT.
EPIDENTIC OF MEASLES AT BuRroNWOOD.

Dr. SEMITON reported that during the month there had been 32 births and 34 deaths. The death-rate was equal to 333 per 1,000 as against 25 the average of the past three months and 28 for the corresponding period of last year. Twenty-four of the deaths occurred at the County Asylum, excluding which the death rate proper for the district was 9.7 per 1,000. An epidemic of measles bad broken out at Burtonwood and 81 children were absent from the Roman Catholic schools. He ordered the closing of that institution for a fort- night and as at the end of that time twenty additional cases had occurred he ordered a further closure for two weeks. The report was approved.

For an array of adjectives the following sentence would, we imagine, be hard to beat. It was uttered by Sir James Barr in the course of his presidential address at the Health Congress at Douglas on Mon- day :—" We must raise up a healthy, strong, sound, vigorous, well-developed, temperate, active, athletic, adventurous, brave, bold, brisk, busy, courageous, chivalrous, daring, defiant, energetic, absolutely fear- less, quick, strenuous, animated, attractive, agile, frolicsome, gallant, gay, jovial, lively, manly, merry, obedient, sportive, vivacious, intellectual, alert, assiduous, confident, diligent, dexterous, enterprising, expert, intrepid, industrious, patient, potent, power- ful, resolute, reliant, skilful, undaunted, valiant, vigilant, benevolent, courtly, courteous, charitable, dignified, elegant, graceful, honourable, kindly, moral, polite, magnanimous, refined, stately, valorous, virtuous, all the other noble qualifications, and last, but not least, a religious and God-fearing race.

" scratCh " meeting has been quite a feature of e Jarrow election. These meetings are held with- out any previous notice, not even the chalk-writing na the footpath. The orator comes along with his borrowed egg box and plants it down by the kerb in,a quiet street, but within sight of the main thoroughfare. He mounts his platform and begins to speak to the universe. There are, perhaps, not more than three or four men within earshot, but they draw near and forn? the nucleus of i meeting which grows by twos ana threes until there are several hundred people in the crowd, almost all men. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Cricket. Rain interfered with Warrington's match with Prescot on Saturday and makes their task of securing the championship all the more difficult as instead of a possible two points they are able only to count one. St. Helens navy claims a clear lead of three points and will take a great deal of ousting from their position. The League tables for the first and second divisions are : FIRST DIVISION. Club P. W. L. D. Pts. St. Helens Warrington Earlestown Prescot 7 3 3 1 7 St. Helens Rees Stanley Newton SECOND DIVISION. Earlestown Prescot Warrington St. Helens Recs. 8 3 4 1 7 St. Helens 6 3 3 0 6 Newton Stanley -- Warrington second were more favoured in regard to weather and avenged a defeat in the earlier part of the season by handsomely beating Prescot second. The visitors batted first and two wickets fell very quickly then a stand was made and by vigorous hitting Birchall and Lyon made the score assume more respect- able proportions. Neither played ideal cricket and both were badly missed in the long field off Plinston. Jones added 30 and the Prescot innings closed for 146. The most successful bowler W 93 Plinston with 7 for 5S and but for mistakes in the field his figures would have been much better. Hawtin took two for six. Waywell did not succeed in getting a single wicket and would probably have met with some success had he kept a better length. -- Hawtin and Thewlis opened the Warrington innings. Both men have done welt during the season and great th,ings were expected. Hawtin opened with confidence but Jones completely beat him and Houghton took his place. Thewlis was not long in getting his eye in and once he had aecomplished this he hit out with great freedom and always had the mastery of the bowling. Not so the other men, amongst whom R. G. Pierpoint (18) was the only one to do anything. Thewlis was the eighth to leave and by that time had secured 84. Singu- larly enough he was the top scorer in the opening match against Prescot with 16, and in 6 completed inxings he has run up a total of 207. For once in a way Orford Barracks have been deposed from the leadership of the Warrington and District League, giving place to St. James' but whether the latter club will succeed in retaining the coveted honour remains to be seen. On Saturday they had a somewhat farcical game with Bevvsey Wesleyans, as only six of their opponents turned out. Of course they won easily. -- Walker's Brewery have at last won a match, this being at the expense of the Wilderspool Brewery team. They are evidently fond of close finishes, as on one occasion they lost by one run, whilst on Saturday the respective totals were 36 and 35. -- Mackie's visited Liverpool on Saturday and secured a victory over Walton St. Mary's. The home team could do nothing with the bowling of Burrell, and were all out for 39. In reply the printers ran up 78 for 7. --- Penketh come a cropper when matched against the Liverpool Strollers and lost by 38. The visitors ran up 6S by a series of small scores and whilst five of the Penketh men bagged ducks. Davies with 11 was the principal scorer for the home team. -- Helsby took the field with only nine men at moore on Saturday and all were out for 19, S. Taylor taking five wickets for seven runs. This score was passed by Moore and Daresbury with several wickets in hand. Dutton hit out well for 27, -- Latchford were unfortunate in being minus six of their regular team on Saturday, but despite this, recorded a very creditable draw with South Rusholme. The home team batted first and compiled a total of 82, of which W. Bennett and S. Albinson each made 22, Jordan and Cox also batting well. The visitors opened rather indifferently, losing 3 wickets for 6 runs. But this was too good for the Latchford bowlers to keep up, and eventually they made 62 for 8 wickets, thus being 19 behind with 2 wickets in hand. Swimming. Warrington water polo team entertained the repre- sentatives of Leigh at Warrington on Thursday. On account of the holidays Leigh were only able to place a weak team in the water and were easily defeated by eight goals to one. The Warrington men were not called upon to put forth their full powers, but despite this gave a good exhibition, passing and shooting with commendable accuracy. Next Thursday they will have to go all the way if they are to defeat Everton in the Liverpool and District League. They have the advantage of playing in the Warrington baths and should pall off the match. -- Immediately before Thursday's game the first round of the Warrington Works Squadron Competition was decided. Co-operative Stores defeated Richmond's after a hard race their time being returned at 2min. 35secs. In the other match the holders of the Gilbert IGreenall Challenge Trophy, Pearson and Knowles met Crosfields, the winners in 1905 and successfully defended their title. Their time was 2min. 22secs. In the 50 yards junior members handicap H. Harding won by a few feet, W. Downing being second and T. Smith, third.

THE EXAMINER. JULY 6th. 1907

WARRINGTON BRIDGE. THE FERRO-CONCRETE SCHEME. More Information Wanted. The old question of the erection of a new bridge to take the place of the present inadequate Warrington ' Bridge was again under the consideration of the Town Council on Tuesday evening. The General Purposes Committee had resolved that the Borough Surveyor ! prepare specifications for a ferro-concrete bridge to ; replace Warrington Bridge and also for a new bridge over the river at Howley. 1 The Ai avort moved the adoption of the minutes. Alderman BENNETT moved that the above recom- mendation be referred back. The way in which the 1 Council proposed to go into the scheme was, he said, ; thoroughly inadequate, and did not show a proper appreciation of its importance. He need scarcely say i that he was as anxious as any member of the Council to i see both bridges erected. Both were absolutely neces- sary, and the Council had been remiss in not having them built long ago. If they were to have the new bridges, it was essential that they should have the two best bridges possible. It seemed to him, with all due respect to Mr. Longdin, that they were not going about the matter the best way in getting him to prepare specifications for a scheme which in his (Alderman Bennett's) opinion required very eminent expert knowledge. He did not know whether any plans of the proposed bridges existed—at any rate, he had not seen them—and he was not going to commit himself blindly to preparing specifications for bridges, plans of which he had not seen. If they were to have due regard to the appearance of the town, the bridges should be handsome and thoroughly worthy of the important positions in which they would be placed. The least the oouncil could do was to consult an eminent engineer before getting out specifications. In time past bridges lasted hundreds of years, and they wanted the new bridges to be of that durable character. He did not know whether ferro-concrete was durable. It was a new article and he was told there had been several disastrous failures with reference to the use of the material. At any rate it was only in its experimental stage, and he was not prepared to vote blindly for it without expert advice. He was told that not only had it in some cases been a failure, but that it was only a material which engineers used for various purposes, that there were many manufacturers of it and that the particu- lar bridge suggested to the Corporation was simply one process out of many others. If the Council decided to go in for ferro-concrete, he understood the best plan would be to have designs and specifications prepared and invite tenders from all the people who manufac- tured ferro-concrete and not leave it to one particular firm. It was always a mistake to entrust any matter to the control of anything in the nature of a monopoly. The MAYOR: We are not going to do that. That is the reason why the Borough Surveyor is to prepare specifications. Alderman BENNETT: If you are not all I have to say is that if you are adopting plans prepared by the representative of this particular process, then you are leaving a matter of immense importance to Mr. Longdin who has not had any experience of building bridges of this character and incurring risk which it is not fair should be placed on his shoulders. Mr. Longdin is an admirable man within the limit of bis powers and authority, but he is not a specialist in bridge building. Continuing he said they wanted two bridges of the best appearance and most durable material, if he mentioned as an expert Mr. Webster, it was because that gentle- man was a Warringtonian and everything else being equal, he (Alderman Bennett) had a leaning to his own townsmen. In the earlier stages of both bridges Mr. Webster was consulted, and plans were prepared by him ten or twelve years ago for a bridge at Howley. It was not fair to Mr. Webster to shelve him now and leave the matter in the hands of the Borough Surveyor. The MAYOR : You are quite wrong. Alderman BENNETT : This is one of the most import- ant schemes that could be brought before the Council and we ought to employ expert knowledge. Continu- ing he said that if they did engage an expert it would only be fair to consider Mr. Webster whom they had previously consulted. Councillor TOOLE seconded. Councillor ASHCROFT said he was surprised at Alder- man Bennett. The matter was thrashed out in the General Purposes Committee, and the alderman was speaking not his own opinion but Mr. Webster's in regard to ferro concrete. Whether Alderman Bennett I was an agent of Mr. Webster's he (Councillor Ashcroft) did not know, but at the committee meeting the alder- men read a letter from Mr. Webster condemning con- crete bridges. Alderman BENNETT: He did not condemn them. Councillor ASHCROFT : I don't know whether you are an agent of Mr. Webster's. Alderman BENNETT: You have no right to make such charges and I resent them. The letter I read was simply for the purposes of information and stated certain facts which it was important the Council should know. You have no right to make insinuations of that kind. I have absolutely no interest in this matter any more than you have. I only desire to have the best bridge for the town. Councillor ASHCROFT : Why did he send the letter to you and not to the Town Clerk? Alderman BENNETT: Because lam a personal friend of his and proud of the fact. Councillor PEMBERTON said he did not believe in employing Mr. Webster. They asked him to meet them in a certain matter and he did not. At the same time there was a great deal in what Alderman Bennett said. fle(Councillor Pemberton) would,however, point out at once that a concrete bridge properly constructed was as strong as any the alderman mentioned. The Council need have no fear because at their own doors they had the gigantic Latchford locks which had to stand a greater strain than the bridges would have to stand, there being the pressure of thousands of tons of water, and they were practically made of concrete, only the top coping being of granite. A concrete bridge wanted to be very carefully supervised. They could easily have a bad structure—more easily than in stone. The matter would have been better discussed in the General Purposes Committee. The different companies who erected ferro-concrete bridges had their own particular systems. Would it not;be better to ask each of the companies to tender for a bridge of a certain size and let them submit their own specifications? Then the Borough Surveyor could go through them. The Borough Surveyor was not altogether ignorant of what bridge building by the ferro-concrere process was. If, however, he drew up the specification the companies might not give the guarantee they would otherwise give. The MAYOR: Mr. Longdin says he would not pre- pare the plans. He would write to the people who made the bridges. Everyone would be asked to give a design. The gentleman we are dealing with has done hundreds of thousands of pounds worth. Councillor PEMBSRTON : It is important that we should see he does not make the one mistake with War- rington Bridge. The resolution does not really mean what it says. It would have been better worded" The Borough Surveyor was requested to invite specifications and tenders." Councillor Dr. JOSEPH agreed that when Mr. Longdin had prepared specifications a special meeting of the Committee should be held to decide what kind of bridge they should have. Councillor LORD said he thought the Council was committed to a cantilever bridge, as the resolution sanctioning that scheme had not been reescinded. The MAYOR: There has been a resolution that we should have a cantilever bridge. Councillor LORD: There have been many resolutions. The MAYOR: Yes, there have. I have been fighting over this bridge question about four years, almost night and day. Councillor LORD: I understood you were a strong advocate of cantilevers. The MAYOR: lam a strong advocate and I would sooner have cantilevers to-day than a new bridge. Councillor LORD said he was one of a few who went , to interview Admiral Nares and although the Admiral would not approve of the plans submitted to him,he said he was quite prepared to consider an amended plan. Why the town should be put to an expense of £20,000 to £30,000 for a new bridge when for £1,500 they could improve the bridge for the next fifty years, he failed to understand. A ferro-concrete bridge meant at least £20,000. He did not know whether members of the Council knew that. The MAYOR: It is not true. I can give you the whole of the estimates. Couneillor LORD: lam a member of the sub-com- mittee and have gone into the matter. If you will Rive the figures from the ferro-concrete people, I think they will enlighten the Council. Councillor EVANS : Before passing the resolution we oneht to know something about the cost. The Mlvort : I will withdraw it. I will not be here all night. This closed the discussion and the scheme was once more withdrawn.
